questions.q: A cantilever resin-bonded bridge (Maryland-type or single-retainer ceramic) is considered. What is the most important prognostic factor for its long-term success?
options: Bonding to the canine rather than the central whenever possible, using a rigid connector, and ensuring the pontic is out of heavy excursive contact
Always bonding to both adjacent teeth for more retention
Using base-metal wings with no enamel preparation
Relying on dentin bonding alone
questions.explanation: Evidence (especially from the Zurich group and subsequent studies) shows that single-retainer cantilever ceramic resin-bonded bridges have higher survival than two-retainer designs because differential tooth movement is avoided. Bonding to the canine (when anatomy allows) and keeping the pontic light in excursion further improve prognosis. Rigid connectors and enamel bonding are essential. Two-retainer designs are more prone to debonding of one wing and caries.

title: High-Load Mandibular Molar — Material & Occlusal Design Selection
short: 51M • #30 crown needed • Heavy function • Limited interocclusal space

patient.medical_history: Healthy; history of fractured porcelain on previous PFM crowns; heavy occlusal function and occasional clenching.
patient.chief_complaint: My old crown on the lower right molar broke and I need something that will not fracture again.

clinical_findings.radiographs: #30 has adequate RCT and remaining tooth structure for a 2 mm ferrule; opposing maxillary molar is a zirconia crown; limited interocclusal clearance (~1.2 mm in centric).

guidelines: Material strength and fracture-toughness data (zirconia vs lithium disilicate vs PFM)
Occlusal scheme design for high-load posterior teeth

vignette.demographics: 51-year-old male with history of porcelain fracture under function.
vignette.chief: Replacement of fractured mandibular molar crown with a material and design that resists fracture.
vignette.clinical: Tooth #30 prepared with 2 mm ferrule possible. Limited vertical space. Patient exhibits wear facets and reports clenching during work stress.
vignette.endo: Previous RCT asymptomatic and radiographically acceptable.
vignette.radio: Adequate bone support; no root fracture.

questions.q: Given limited interocclusal space (~1.2 mm) and high functional load, which material and restoration design is most appropriate?
options: Layered lithium disilicate crown with 0.8 mm occlusal thickness
Monolithic zirconia crown with minimal occlusal reduction (following manufacturer minimum thickness) and a refined occlusal scheme that avoids heavy interferences
Feldspathic porcelain jacket crown
Full-contour resin crown as long-term solution
questions.explanation: Monolithic zirconia offers high flexural strength and fracture toughness even at reduced thicknesses, making it suitable for limited interocclusal space and high load. Layered lithium disilicate or feldspathic porcelain have higher chipping/fracture risk under heavy function, especially when thickness is compromised. Resin is not a long-term high-load posterior solution. Current material selection guidelines support monolithic zirconia in this scenario.

questions.q: What occlusal design feature is most important to protect both the restoration and the opposing zirconia crown?
options: Steep cuspal inclines for maximum efficiency
Broad centric contacts on flat or gently contoured fossae, with excursive movements directed to minimize lateral stress and eliminate interferences on the restored molar
Balancing contacts on the molar during laterotrusion
No contacts in centric relation
questions.explanation: Flattened or gently angled occlusal morphology with well-distributed centric contacts reduces peak stresses. Lateral interferences and steep inclines increase the risk of fracture or opposing wear. Balancing contacts on a single molar are generally undesirable in natural dentition or fixed restorations. Proper occlusal design is as important as material choice for longevity under parafunctional load.

questions.q: The patient asks whether a post and core is required because the tooth had root canal treatment. What is the correct evidence-based response?
options: Every endodontically treated molar requires a post
A post is indicated only when remaining coronal tooth structure is insufficient to retain the core; with a 2 mm ferrule and adequate walls, a post is unnecessary and may weaken the root
A post should always be placed to reinforce the tooth against fracture
Only metal posts are acceptable in molars
questions.explanation: Posts do not strengthen teeth; they retain cores when coronal structure is lacking. When sufficient walls and a 2 mm ferrule remain, a bonded core (or even an amalgam or composite core) without a post is preferred. Unnecessary posts remove additional dentin and can increase root fracture risk. This principle is well established in the endodontic–prosthodontic literature.

title: High-Risk Impacted #17 — Inferior Alveolar Nerve Proximity & Coronectomy Decision
short: 28F • ASA I • Deep vertical impaction • CBCT shows canal compression

patient.medical_history: Healthy, no medications, NKDA. Presents for evaluation of recurrent pericoronitis #17.
patient.chief_complaint: Repeated swelling and pain behind my lower left wisdom tooth for the past 8 months.

clinical_findings.exam: Partial soft-tissue impaction #17, mild erythema, probing depth 7 mm distal. No neurosensory deficit. #32 similarly impacted but asymptomatic.
clinical_findings.imaging: Panoramic: deep vertical #17 with loss of white lines of IAN canal and darkening of root. CBCT: canal compressed and lingually diverted by distal root; residual bone above canal <1 mm; no direct interruption of canal cortex.

vignette.demographics: 28-year-old healthy female, ASA I.
vignette.chief: Recurrent pericoronitis associated with partially erupted #17.
vignette.clinical: Soft-tissue impaction, distal probing 7 mm, no paresthesia.
vignette.radio: CBCT confirms intimate relationship of distal root with IAN canal (compression + diversion) without frank canal cortical breach.

questions.q: According to current evidence-based risk stratification, which radiographic finding most strongly elevates the risk of IAN injury and supports consideration of coronectomy rather than complete extraction?
options: Darkening of the root alone on panoramic radiograph
Interruption of the white line of the canal on panoramic film
CBCT demonstration of canal compression with <1–2 mm residual bone and diversion of the canal by the root
Vertical impaction angulation >45 degrees
questions.explanation: While panoramic signs (Rood & Shehab) raise suspicion, CBCT quantification of canal compression, diversion, and residual bone height provides the highest positive predictive value for nerve injury. When the root is intimately related and complete removal would require significant manipulation near the canal, coronectomy (intentional root retention) has Level 2–3 evidence for markedly reduced permanent neurosensory deficit rates while still eliminating the pericoronitis source.

questions.q: If coronectomy is selected, which statement regarding technique and follow-up is most accurate?
options: The pulp must be treated endodontically before root retention
Roots should be left 3–4 mm above the crestal bone to facilitate later retrieval

Enamel and any exposed pulp are reduced so the remaining root is at least 3 mm below the crestal bone; primary soft-tissue closure is preferred; late root migration is monitored but intervention is needed only if exposure or infection occurs
Antibiotics are mandatory for 10 days and the patient must avoid chewing on that side for 6 months
questions.explanation: Standard coronectomy protocol (Pogrel/Renton modifications) requires complete enamel removal and reduction of the root surface so it lies well below the crest, allowing bone and soft tissue to cover it. Pulp treatment is unnecessary; vital roots are well tolerated. Late migration occurs in a minority of cases and is managed only if clinical problems arise. Routine prolonged antibiotics are not evidence-based.

questions.q: Red-team consent point: Which risk must be explicitly discussed and documented when offering coronectomy versus complete removal?
options: Only the risk of dry socket
Possibility of subsequent root migration requiring a second procedure, residual infection, and the residual (though reduced) risk of temporary or permanent neurosensory change
Guaranteed elimination of all future pathology
No additional risks compared with routine extraction
questions.explanation: Coronectomy is a risk-reduction strategy, not risk elimination. Patients must understand that a second procedure may be required if the retained root becomes exposed or symptomatic, that infection can still occur, and that temporary or permanent nerve injury remains possible (though significantly less frequent than with high-risk complete extraction). Failure to document this shared decision-making is a common source of later dissatisfaction or claims.

title: Stage 2 Medication-Related Osteonecrosis of the Jaw (Denosumab) — Management Sequencing
short: 68F • Metastatic breast cancer • Denosumab • Exposed bone 8 weeks

patient.medical_history: Metastatic breast cancer on denosumab 120 mg SC q4 weeks for 18 months; prior zoledronic acid for 2 years. No radiation. HbA1c 6.4%. On anastrozole.
patient.chief_complaint: Pain and exposed bone in the lower right jaw after a dental cleaning 3 months ago; antibiotics have not resolved it.

clinical_findings.exam: 2.5 cm area of exposed necrotic bone buccal and lingual #30–31 region, purulent drainage, soft-tissue erythema, no extraoral fistula, no neurosensory change. #30 has Class II mobility.
clinical_findings.imaging: CBCT: mixed osteolysis and sclerosis of the right mandibular body with sequestra; periosteal reaction; no pathologic fracture. Stage 2 MRONJ.

vignette.demographics: 68-year-old female with metastatic breast cancer on long-term denosumab (and prior IV bisphosphonate).
vignette.chief: Exposed bone and pain after dental prophylaxis.
vignette.clinical: Exposed necrotic bone with infection (Stage 2), mobile adjacent tooth.
vignette.radio: CBCT confirms osteonecrosis with sequestra, no fracture.

questions.q: According to the 2022 AAOMS Position Paper, what is the preferred initial management approach for Stage 2 MRONJ in this patient?
options: Immediate segmental resection and reconstruction plate

Conservative therapy: antimicrobial mouth rinses, systemic antibiotics for acute infection, superficial debridement of mobile sequestra, and pain control; surgery reserved for progression or refractory disease
Hyperbaric oxygen as first-line monotherapy
Immediate drug holiday for 12 months then wide resection
questions.explanation: AAOMS 2022 continues to support stage-specific therapy. Stage 2 (exposed bone + infection) is managed primarily with local care, antibiotics directed at the infection, and removal of only mobile necrotic fragments. Aggressive resection is reserved for Stage 3 or refractory Stage 2. Hyperbaric oxygen has insufficient evidence as primary therapy. Drug interruption decisions require oncology collaboration and are not automatic.

questions.q: Regarding interruption of denosumab, which statement is most consistent with current multi-disciplinary guidance?
options: Denosumab must be stopped for at least 6 months before any oral surgical intervention

Because denosumab has a shorter half-life than bisphosphonates, a brief interruption (in consultation with the oncologist) may be considered, but the anti-resorptive effect dissipates more rapidly and rebound bone turnover is a concern; decisions are individualized
Denosumab never needs to be interrupted because MRONJ risk is lower than with zoledronic acid
Switch immediately to an oral bisphosphonate
questions.explanation: Denosumab’s reversible effect on RANKL allows the theoretical possibility of a drug holiday with recovery of bone remodeling, unlike the long skeletal half-life of IV bisphosphonates. However, oncology teams must weigh skeletal-related event risk versus MRONJ healing potential. There is no universal mandatory holiday; decisions are case-by-case with the prescribing oncologist. Rebound vertebral fractures after denosumab cessation are a recognized concern.

questions.q: If the exposed area progresses to Stage 3 (pathologic fracture or extraoral fistula), what surgical principle is currently favored when resection is required?
options: Minimal curettage only

Resection to bleeding bone margins with primary soft-tissue coverage; reconstruction deferred or performed with vascularized tissue when continuity is lost, coordinated with oncology regarding timing of anti-resorptive restart
Immediate free-flap reconstruction in every case regardless of disease status
Extraction of all remaining teeth in the jaw
questions.explanation: Stage 3 disease often requires segmental or marginal resection to viable (bleeding) bone. Soft-tissue coverage is essential. Reconstruction timing and method depend on oncologic prognosis, defect size, and whether anti-resorptive therapy will continue. Prophylactic extraction of all teeth is not supported.

title: Mandibular Angle Fracture with Third Molar in the Line of Fracture
short: 22M • Assault • Left angle fracture • #17 in fracture line

patient.medical_history: Previously healthy, social ethanol use, no regular medications.
patient.chief_complaint: Punched in the jaw 6 hours ago; malocclusion and pain on the left side.

clinical_findings.exam: Left facial swelling, step deformity at inferior border, V3 sensation intact, limited opening 25 mm, premature contact on left posterior, #17 partially erupted and mobile within the fracture line. No floor-of-mouth elevation.
clinical_findings.imaging: CT: non-displaced to minimally displaced left mandibular angle fracture through the socket of #17; second fracture at right parasymphysis (minimally displaced).

guidelines: Evidence on third-molar retention vs removal in angle fractures

vignette.demographics: 22-year-old male, assault victim, 6 hours post-injury.
vignette.chief: Malocclusion and pain after blow to jaw.
vignette.clinical: Angle + parasymphysis fractures, #17 in line of left angle fracture, intact neurosensory function.
vignette.radio: CT confirms angle fracture involving #17 socket and contralateral parasymphysis fracture.

questions.q: Regarding the third molar in the line of the angle fracture, what is the current evidence-based recommendation?
options: Always extract the tooth at the time of ORIF to reduce infection risk
Always retain the tooth because extraction weakens the fracture reduction

Decision is individualized: retain if the tooth is restorable, not fractured, and does not interfere with reduction; extract if it is grossly carious, fractured, mobile and preventing reduction, or has advanced periodontitis
Delay all decisions until 6 weeks after ORIF
questions.explanation: Contemporary literature and AAOMS guidance support selective management. Teeth that aid reduction and are otherwise healthy may be retained and later restored or electively removed. Teeth that are a source of infection, prevent anatomic reduction, or are non-restorable are removed at the time of ORIF. Routine extraction of every tooth in the line of fracture is no longer mandated.

questions.q: Preferred fixation strategy for a non-comminuted mandibular angle fracture treated via intraoral approach is:
options: Maxillomandibular fixation alone for 6 weeks
Single superior-border miniplate along Champy lines (load-sharing) with or without a second plate if needed for stability
Reconstruction plate from the extraoral approach in every angle fracture
Lag-screw fixation only
questions.explanation: For non-comminuted angle fractures, Champy’s ideal osteosynthesis lines allow a single superior-border miniplate to function in a load-sharing manner when the fracture is adequately reduced. A second plate may be added for additional stability. Reconstruction plates and extraoral approaches are reserved for comminuted, atrophic, or infected fractures. MMF alone has higher complication rates for angle fractures.

questions.q: Red-team perioperative concern: What is the most important early postoperative instruction to reduce the risk of hardware failure or malunion in this young adult?
options: Immediate unrestricted chewing
Strict non-chew / soft diet for the prescribed period, oral hygiene with irrigating devices, and early reporting of any change in occlusion or increased pain
Mandatory 6 weeks of tight MMF regardless of fixation
Prophylactic extraction of the contralateral third molar during the same anesthetic
questions.explanation: Even with rigid fixation, early excessive loading is a common cause of plate fracture or non-union at the angle. Clear dietary restriction, hygiene to prevent infection at the fracture site, and prompt evaluation of occlusal change are essential. Routine contralateral third-molar removal is not required for fracture management.

title: Deep Space Odontogenic Infection — Threat to Airway
short: 34M • Uncontrolled T2DM • Rapidly progressive submandibular / sublingual swelling

patient.medical_history: Type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 11.2%), no routine care, presents 4 days after onset of toothache #17.
patient.chief_complaint: Cannot swallow saliva, tongue feels pushed up, fever and chills.

clinical_findings.exam: Toxic appearance, temperature 39.1 °C, floor-of-mouth elevated and firm, tongue elevated and protruded, bilateral submandibular swelling, trismus 15 mm, stridor when supine. #17 gross caries with vestibular fluctuance.
clinical_findings.imaging: CT with contrast: multi-loculated abscess involving left submandibular, sublingual, and lateral pharyngeal spaces; airway narrowed at oropharyngeal level.

vignette.demographics: 34-year-old male with poorly controlled diabetes.
vignette.chief: Inability to swallow, elevated tongue, systemic toxicity after neglected odontogenic infection.
vignette.clinical: Elevated floor of mouth, trismus, stridor — impending airway compromise.
vignette.radio: CT confirms multi-space abscess with airway narrowing.

questions.q: Immediate priority in this patient’s management is:
options: IV antibiotics alone and observation
Urgent airway assessment and securement (often fiber-optic or awake tracheostomy if difficult), followed by prompt incision and drainage and source removal under controlled conditions
Extraction of #17 in the clinic chair under local anesthesia
CT-guided aspiration only
questions.explanation: Airway is the first priority in any deep-space infection with floor-of-mouth elevation and stridor. Once the airway is secure, definitive source control (incision, drainage of all involved spaces, and extraction of the offending tooth) is performed. Antibiotics are adjunctive, not definitive. Clinic extraction under local is dangerous and inadequate.

questions.q: Which statement regarding antibiotic selection while awaiting culture is most appropriate?
options: Oral penicillin VK is sufficient

Broad-spectrum IV coverage directed at oral streptococci, anaerobes, and possible Gram-negatives (e.g., ampicillin-sulbactam or piperacillin-tazobactam ± vancomycin if MRSA risk), adjusted once cultures return
Antifungal therapy must be started empirically
No antibiotics are needed if drainage is performed
questions.explanation: Severe multi-space infections in a diabetic host require immediate broad IV coverage of the expected polymicrobial oral flora. Culture-directed de-escalation follows. Antifungals are not first-line. Drainage without antibiotics risks continued bacteremia in a compromised host.

questions.q: Red-team systems issue: What is the most common management error that leads to airway catastrophe in similar presentations?
options: Obtaining CT before any clinical airway evaluation
Underestimating the speed of progression and attempting a ‘quick look’ under inadequate anesthesia without a surgical airway backup plan
Giving steroids
Using too much local anesthetic
questions.explanation: Patients with evolving floor-of-mouth and lateral pharyngeal collections can progress from stable to complete obstruction rapidly. The classic error is proceeding to the OR or attempting intubation without a ready surgical airway plan and without recognizing that standard laryngoscopy may be impossible. Early involvement of anesthesia and OMFS with explicit airway strategy prevents fatalities.

title: Suspicious Oral Lesion — Biopsy Decision & Staging Pathway
short: 61M • 30 pack-year smoker • Non-healing ulcer lateral tongue 8 weeks

patient.medical_history: 30 pack-year smoking history, social alcohol, hypertension on lisinopril, no prior oral cancer.
patient.chief_complaint: Sore on the side of my tongue that has not healed for two months; now it bleeds easily.

clinical_findings.exam: 2.2 cm indurated, non-homogeneous ulcer on left lateral tongue with surrounding erythroplakia; firm, mobile Level II lymph node 1.5 cm on the ipsilateral neck. No trismus, no tongue fixation.

vignette.demographics: 61-year-old male smoker with a non-healing lateral tongue ulcer.
vignette.chief: Persistent painful ulcer that bleeds.
vignette.clinical: Indurated ulcer + ipsilateral suspicious lymphadenopathy.
vignette.radio: Imaging pending definitive tissue diagnosis.

questions.q: The most appropriate next diagnostic step is:
options: Empiric antifungal therapy for 2 weeks and re-evaluate

Incisional biopsy of the most representative (indurated, non-necrotic) area of the lesion, preferably including the interface with adjacent mucosa, performed in a manner that does not compromise future resection margins
Excisional biopsy of the entire lesion in the office
Immediate hemiglossectomy based on clinical appearance
questions.explanation: Any non-healing ulcer in a high-risk patient requires timely tissue diagnosis. Incisional biopsy of the most abnormal area is preferred so that the pathologist receives adequate tissue while the surgeon preserves the ability to perform a definitive oncologic resection later. Complete office excision of a lesion this size risks positive margins and complicates subsequent therapy. Empiric therapy only delays diagnosis.

questions.q: Assuming squamous-cell carcinoma is confirmed, which staging investigation is required before definitive treatment planning?
options: Panoramic radiograph only
Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the neck (and primary) plus evaluation for distant disease per NCCN (CT chest or PET/CT as indicated by stage and clinical risk)
No imaging is necessary if the lesion is <3 cm
Bone scan as the sole study
questions.explanation: AJCC/NCCN staging for oral cavity SCC requires accurate assessment of primary extent, depth of invasion (pathologic), and regional nodes. Cross-sectional imaging of the neck is mandatory; chest imaging is added for pulmonary staging. PET/CT is often used for more advanced lesions. Under-staging by omitting imaging leads to inadequate treatment.

questions.q: Red-team communication point: When discussing the biopsy result with the patient, which approach best supports informed decision-making?
options: Tell the patient ‘it is probably nothing’ to avoid worry

Provide clear information about diagnosis, the need for multi-disciplinary evaluation (surgery, radiation oncology, medical oncology as indicated), expected treatment pathway, and the importance of smoking cessation, while allowing time for questions
Refer immediately without further discussion
Recommend alternative medicine first
questions.explanation: Delivering a cancer diagnosis requires honesty, empathy, and a structured explanation of next steps. Multi-disciplinary care is standard. Smoking cessation counseling is both therapeutic and prognostic. Minimizing the finding or abandoning the patient damages trust and outcomes.

title: Severe Odontogenic Maxillary Sinusitis & Failed Implant — Combined Rhinologic / Surgical Approach
short: 55M • Chronic sinusitis after posterior maxillary implant • Oro-antral communication

patient.medical_history: Hypertension, remote history of #3 extraction and immediate implant placement 4 years earlier; progressive left nasal congestion and foul drainage for 14 months.
patient.chief_complaint: Constant left nasal obstruction, post-nasal drip with foul taste, and intermittent swelling over the left cheek.

clinical_findings.exam: Mild left mid-face tenderness, purulent drainage from left middle meatus, 4 mm oro-antral fistula at the #3 implant site with peri-implant mucosal inflammation. Implant has Class II mobility.
clinical_findings.imaging: CBCT: complete opacification of left maxillary sinus, osteitis of the sinus floor around the implant apex, which protrudes 4 mm into the sinus; patent osteomeatal complex on the right, obstructed on the left.

guidelines: AAOMS / ARS consensus on odontogenic sinusitis

vignette.demographics: 55-year-old male with chronic left sinus symptoms years after posterior maxillary implant.
vignette.chief: Foul nasal drainage and cheek pressure.
vignette.clinical: Mobile implant, oro-antral fistula, endoscopic evidence of sinusitis.
vignette.radio: CBCT shows implant protrusion into a completely opacified left maxillary sinus.

questions.q: The most evidence-based definitive management sequence is:
options: Long-term oral antibiotics and observation
Removal of the failed implant, closure of the oro-antral communication, and functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) to restore drainage — preferably coordinated between OMFS and otolaryngology
Only endoscopic sinus surgery leaving the implant in place
Immediate zygomatic implants to bypass the sinus
questions.explanation: Odontogenic sinusitis caused by a failed implant will not resolve until the foreign body and source of contamination are removed and the sinus drainage pathway is restored. Combined oral surgical removal + fistula closure + FESS has the highest success rates in the current literature. Antibiotics alone or FESS alone leave the etiology untreated.

questions.q: At the time of implant removal and fistula closure, which soft-tissue technique is most predictable for a 4–5 mm chronic oro-antral communication?
options: Simple interrupted sutures only
Buccal advancement flap or buccal fat pad pedicled flap (alone or in combination), with tension-free closure and consideration of a membrane or graft if the bony defect is large
Primary intention without flap mobilization
Immediate soft-tissue grafting from the palate without addressing the sinus
questions.explanation: Chronic fistulas require tension-free, well-vascularized soft-tissue closure. Buccal advancement and buccal fat pad flaps are workhorse techniques with high success when the sinus pathology is simultaneously addressed. Simple sutures on residual inflamed tissue have high failure rates.

questions.q: Red-team planning point: Before any reconstructive implant therapy is reconsidered in this quadrant, what must be confirmed?
options: That the patient simply wants implants again

Complete resolution of sinus disease (clinical + radiographic), mature soft-tissue closure, and adequate residual bone or staged grafting potential; otherwise alternative prosthetic plans should be offered
Immediate placement of a longer implant
No further imaging is ever needed
questions.explanation: Re-implantation into a previously infected, surgically violated sinus without documented resolution of disease and soft-tissue stability invites recurrent sinusitis and implant failure. Patients must be given realistic alternatives (removable partial, fixed dental prosthesis from adjacent teeth, or zygomatic options only after sinus health is restored).

title: Palatally Impacted Maxillary Canine — CBCT Risk Stratification & Traction Sequencing
short: 14F • delayed eruption #11 • palatal bulge • CBCT

patient.medical_history: Healthy, no medications, NKDA. No family history of dental anomalies.
patient.chief_complaint: My upper right permanent canine still has not come in and the baby tooth is getting loose.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: Primary canine (#53) present with Grade 2 mobility; permanent canine not palpable buccally; slight palatal bulge.
clinical_findings.mobility: Normal elsewhere; no pathologic mobility of adjacent teeth.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Panoramic shows #11 (permanent canine) overlapping the root of #12 on 2D imaging. CBCT confirms mid-palatal impaction, crown apex distal to #12 root, no root resorption of lateral incisor, adequate bone for closed exposure.

flags: No lateral-incisor root resorption on CBCT
guidelines: AAO Clinical Practice Guidelines — Impacted Canines
CBCT for localization and resorption assessment (AAOMR/AAO)
Closed vs open surgical exposure evidence

vignette.demographics: 14-year-old female, healthy, no medications, NKDA.
vignette.chief: Delayed eruption of the permanent maxillary right canine; primary canine still present and mobile.
vignette.clinical: Palatal bulge in the region of #11; no buccal palpation of the canine crown. Primary #53 Grade 2 mobility. Adjacent teeth periodontally healthy.
vignette.endo: N/A — all teeth vital; no history of trauma.
vignette.radio: CBCT: mid-palatal impaction of #11, crown positioned apical and slightly distal to the root of #12, no evidence of lateral-incisor root resorption, sufficient bone for closed-eruption technique.

questions.q: According to current AAO/AAOMR guidance, what is the primary justification for obtaining CBCT rather than relying solely on panoramic + occlusal radiographs in this case?
options: CBCT is required for every unerupted tooth
To determine exact 3-D position, proximity to adjacent roots, and presence/absence of resorption that will dictate surgical approach and traction vector
Only to measure bone density for implant planning
Panoramic imaging is always sufficient for localization
questions.explanation: 2-D imaging suffers from superimposition. CBCT provides the precise labiolingual position, relationship to the lateral-incisor root, and quantifies any resorption. These data directly determine whether a closed or open exposure is preferred and the direction of orthodontic traction. AAOMR/AAO position papers support limited-field CBCT when the information will change treatment.

questions.q: The preferred surgical-orthodontic approach for a mid-palatal canine without lateral-incisor resorption in a cooperative adolescent is:
options: Extract the permanent canine and place an implant later
Open surgical exposure with free gingival graft and immediate traction
Closed surgical exposure with bonded attachment and light continuous traction after primary-canine extraction
Wait until age 18 and reassess
questions.explanation: Closed eruption technique is favored for mid-palatal impactions because it produces a more physiologic gingival attachment and better long-term periodontal outcomes. Light, continuous force (typically <60 g) after extraction of the primary canine is the evidence-based traction protocol. Open exposure is more often reserved for labially positioned canines or when the crown is superficial.

questions.q: Red-team risk point: What is the most important factor that would cause you to abandon traction and consider extraction of the impacted canine?
options: Patient is 14 years old
CBCT evidence of significant (>50 %) lateral-incisor root resorption or ankylosis of the canine itself
Slight distal crown position
Presence of a primary canine
questions.explanation: Severe root resorption of the adjacent lateral already present, or radiographic/clinical signs of ankylosis of the canine, markedly worsen the risk–benefit ratio of prolonged traction. In such situations extraction of the canine (and possible autotransplantation or prosthetic replacement) becomes the more predictable option. Age alone or minor positional variations are not absolute contraindications.

title: Growing Class II Division 1 — Functional Appliance vs Extraction Camouflage Decision
short: 11M • ANB 7° • horizontal growth • full Class II molars

patient.medical_history: Healthy, athletic, no medications. Mother reports he is a mouth-breather at night.
patient.chief_complaint: My front teeth stick out and I get teased at school.

clinical_findings.radiographs: Lateral cephalogram: SNA 82°, SNB 75°, ANB 7°, FMA 22°, short mandibular ramus, convex profile, competent lips at rest only with strain. Hand-wrist: MP3 stage (peak velocity approaching).

guidelines: Timing relative to pubertal growth spurt

vignette.demographics: 11-year-old male, healthy, athletic, mild nocturnal mouth-breathing reported.
vignette.chief: Protrusive maxillary incisors and social teasing.
vignette.clinical: Full-cusp Class II molars and canines bilaterally, 8 mm overjet, 60 % overbite, mild crowding lower arch, convex soft-tissue profile with lip strain on closure.
vignette.endo: All teeth vital; no trauma history.
vignette.radio: Ceph: ANB 7°, low FMA, short ramus. Hand-wrist indicates patient is entering the peak height-velocity window.

questions.q: Given the cephalometric and maturational findings, the most evidence-based initial approach is:
options: Immediate extraction of maxillary first premolars and fixed appliance camouflage
Growth modification with a functional appliance (Twin-block or Herbst-type) timed to the pubertal growth spurt, followed by fixed appliances
Wait until age 16 and then plan orthognathic surgery
Maxillary skeletal expander alone
questions.explanation: In a growing patient with a horizontal pattern and significant mandibular deficiency who is entering the peak growth velocity window, functional appliance therapy has the highest probability of producing clinically useful mandibular growth contribution and improvement in soft-tissue profile. Premolar extraction camouflage is reserved for non-growing patients or those who decline growth modification. Early surgery is not indicated.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects current evidence regarding the long-term skeletal contribution of functional appliances?
options: They produce large, stable increases in mandibular length that permanently eliminate the need for later surgery
They produce modest skeletal change plus significant dentoalveolar effects; a portion of the Class II correction is often lost without careful retention and growth monitoring
They have zero skeletal effect and work only by proclining lower incisors
They are contraindicated in horizontal growers
questions.explanation: High-quality trials and systematic reviews show that functional appliances produce a combination of modest true skeletal change and larger dentoalveolar compensations. Some of the correction is lost post-treatment, especially if residual growth is unfavorable. Realistic informed consent must reflect this mixed outcome rather than promising large permanent skeletal gains.

questions.q: Red-team airway consideration: How should the reported nocturnal mouth-breathing influence the orthodontic plan?
options: Ignore it — airway is outside the orthodontist’s scope
Screen with pediatric sleep questionnaire / refer for ENT or sleep evaluation before or concurrent with functional appliance therapy; address nasal obstruction if present
Immediately prescribe a mandibular advancement device for OSA
Extract premolars to reduce overjet and thereby improve airway
questions.explanation: Mouth-breathing may reflect adenoidal or turbinate obstruction that can affect growth pattern and treatment stability. Current interdisciplinary standards require screening and, when indicated, referral before or during growth-modification therapy. Functional appliances themselves are not first-line OSA therapy in children; the underlying nasal airway must be evaluated.

title: Adult Orthodontics with Reduced Periodontium — Interdisciplinary Staging
short: 48F • Stage III perio history • 5 mm crowding • wants alignment

patient.medical_history: Former smoker (quit 8 years), well-controlled hypertension (amlodipine). History of scaling & root planing and regenerative surgery #19, #30 five years ago. Currently on 3-month perio maintenance.
patient.chief_complaint: I want my lower front teeth straightened; they have been shifting since my gum treatment.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: Residual 4–5 mm pockets #19, #30; otherwise ≤3 mm. Bleeding on probing localized. Clinical attachment loss 4–6 mm lower anterior.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Horizontal bone loss 20–30 % lower anterior; vertical defects previously grafted at molars show fill. No active caries.

flags: Stage III periodontitis, currently stable on maintenance
guidelines: Light-force protocols and retention in adults

vignette.demographics: 48-year-old female, former smoker, controlled hypertension, history of Stage III periodontitis now on 3-month maintenance.
vignette.chief: Progressive lower anterior crowding and desire for alignment.
vignette.clinical: Stable residual probing depths, localized BOP, Grade 1 mobility lower incisors, 5 mm irregular crowding, thin phenotype.
vignette.endo: All teeth vital; previous endodontic treatment #19 is asymptomatic.
vignette.radio: Moderate horizontal bone loss lower anterior; stable grafted sites at mandibular molars.

questions.q: Before any orthodontic tooth movement is initiated, the mandatory prerequisite is:
options: Immediate fixed appliance placement to ‘stabilize’ the teeth
Documented periodontal stability (no progressive attachment loss, controlled inflammation) for at least 3–6 months and a coordinated perio-ortho treatment plan
Extraction of the most mobile incisors
Systemic antibiotics for 2 weeks
questions.explanation: Orthodontic movement through an inflamed or unstable periodontium accelerates attachment loss. Current perio-ortho consensus requires inflammation control and demonstrated stability before active tooth movement. A written interdisciplinary plan that defines force levels, hygiene protocol, and retention is essential.

questions.q: Which biomechanical principle is most critical when moving teeth with reduced periodontal support?
options: Heavy continuous forces to ‘speed up’ treatment
Light, controlled forces, longer inter-appointment intervals, and absolute avoidance of round-tripping or uncontrolled tipping
Only clear aligners are safe
No special modifications are needed
questions.explanation: Reduced bone support increases stress on the remaining PDL. Light forces, careful moment-to-force ratios, and avoidance of reciprocal round-tripping minimize the risk of further attachment loss and mobility. Clear aligners are not inherently safer; the force system and periodontal control matter more than the appliance type.

questions.q: Red-team long-term risk: After alignment is achieved, what retention strategy is most appropriate for lower anterior teeth with reduced periodontium and prior mobility?
options: Removable Hawley worn only at night for 6 months
Bonded fixed lingual retainer (with careful hygiene access) + periodic perio-ortho monitoring for life
No retention is needed once the teeth are straight
Extract and replace with an implant-supported FPD
questions.explanation: Teeth with reduced support and previous mobility have a high relapse potential. A bonded lingual retainer provides continuous stability while still allowing hygiene. Lifelong monitoring is required because the periodontium remains compromised. Short-term removable retention alone is insufficient in this risk profile.

title: Severe External Apical Root Resorption During Active Treatment
short: 16F • 9 months into fixed treatment • blunted apices upper incisors

patient.medical_history: Healthy, no medications. History of prior trauma to #8 and #9 at age 9 (uncomplicated crown fractures restored).
patient.chief_complaint: Routine progress records show short roots on the upper front teeth.

clinical_findings.radiographs: Progress panoramic + periapicals: #8 and #9 now exhibit severe external apical root resorption (loss of >1/3 original length); other teeth mild blunting. Cephalometric goals not yet fully achieved.

flags: History of trauma to the same teeth
guidelines: Risk factors for EARR (trauma history, genetics, force magnitude)
Decision algorithms for treatment modification or cessation

vignette.demographics: 16-year-old female, healthy, history of childhood trauma to maxillary central incisors.
vignette.chief: Radiographic discovery of significant root shortening during routine progress evaluation.
vignette.clinical: Teeth asymptomatic, vital, normal mobility, healthy gingival tissues. Fixed appliances present.
vignette.endo: Pulp vitality testing within normal limits; no sinus tracts or swelling.
vignette.radio: Severe external apical root resorption #8 and #9 (>1/3 root length lost); mild blunting elsewhere.

questions.q: What is the most appropriate immediate management step once severe EARR is identified?
options: Continue treatment unchanged to finish as quickly as possible
Pause active tooth movement of the affected teeth, obtain high-quality periapicals or limited CBCT, inform the patient/parents, and re-evaluate the cost–benefit of further movement
Immediately extract the resorbed teeth
Increase force levels to finish faster
questions.explanation: Continued heavy or prolonged movement of teeth already showing severe resorption risks further loss and potential tooth loss. Standard of care is to stop or dramatically reduce forces on the affected teeth, document, discuss risks with the family, and decide whether limited finishing, early debond, or acceptance of residual malocclusion is the safer path.

questions.q: Which pre-treatment factor most strongly increased this patient’s risk for severe EARR?
options: Female sex alone
Previous trauma to the maxillary central incisors
Use of nickel-titanium wires
Extraction of premolars
questions.explanation: A history of trauma is one of the strongest identifiable risk factors for external apical root resorption during orthodontic treatment. Other recognized factors include genetic predisposition, prolonged treatment, and heavy continuous forces, but prior trauma is the most relevant in this vignette.

questions.q: Red-team informed-consent point: If treatment is stopped early because of severe EARR, what must be documented and communicated?
options: That root resorption never progresses after appliance removal
That the teeth remain at elevated lifelong risk of further mobility or loss, that restorative or prosthetic implications may arise, and that long-term radiographic follow-up is required
That implants should be placed immediately
That no further dental care is needed
questions.explanation: Even after forces cease, previously resorbed teeth carry a higher long-term risk of mobility, fracture, or loss. Patients and parents must understand residual malocclusion, possible future restorative needs, and the necessity of periodic radiographic monitoring. Failure to disclose these risks is a common source of later medicolegal conflict.

title: Clear Aligner Limitations — Severe Rotation & Vertical Movement Request
short: 32M • 45° rotation #7 • 3 mm extrusion needed #10 • aligner only request

patient.medical_history: Healthy, no medications, non-smoker. Previous orthodontics as a teenager with subsequent relapse.
patient.chief_complaint: I only want clear aligners. I refuse metal braces. Can you fix the rotated tooth and the high lateral?

clinical_findings.radiographs: Full-mouth series and panoramic within normal limits; adequate root length; no pathology.

flags: History of relapse after prior orthodontics

vignette.demographics: 32-year-old male, healthy, previous adolescent orthodontics with relapse.
vignette.chief: Wants correction of a severely rotated maxillary lateral and a high contralateral lateral using only clear aligners.
vignette.clinical: #7 rotated approximately 45°, #10 supra-erupted 3 mm relative to the occlusal plane, mild crowding, Class I molars, healthy periodontium.
vignette.radio: Normal root morphology and bone levels; no contraindications to tooth movement.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects current evidence on clear-aligner predictability for the movements requested?
options: Rotations >30° and pure extrusion are among the most predictable aligner movements
Severe rotations and extrusion are among the least predictable movements with aligners alone; hybrid mechanics or fixed appliances are often required for reliable outcomes
Aligners can predictably correct any movement if enough attachments are used
Only extraction cases are unpredictable with aligners
questions.explanation: Multiple studies and systematic reviews consistently rank pure extrusion and rotations greater than ~30° as low-predictability movements with clear aligners. Attachments and over-corrections improve results but do not eliminate the biomechanical limitation. Honest consent requires disclosure that hybrid treatment (aligners + sectional fixed or auxiliaries) may be necessary.

questions.q: If the patient continues to refuse any fixed appliances, the most ethically appropriate next step is:
options: Proceed with aligners and promise ideal results
Decline treatment entirely
Provide detailed informed consent about limited predictability, possible need for refinement or compromise, and document the discussion; consider a limited trial or referral
Extract the rotated tooth and place an implant
questions.explanation: Autonomy allows a patient to refuse fixed appliances, but the clinician must not promise outcomes the appliance is unlikely to deliver. Thorough informed consent, documentation of limitations, and either a cautious trial with clear decision points or referral to a provider willing to accept the compromised goal are the ethically sound paths.

questions.q: Red-team retention concern given the history of prior relapse: What additional measure should be planned from the outset?
options: No retention is needed with aligners
Long-term (possibly indefinite) bonded or vacuum-formed retention, especially for the rotated and extruded teeth, with explicit patient education about lifelong compliance
Only three months of retention
Circumferential supracrestal fiberotomy is never indicated
questions.explanation: Rotated teeth and previously relapsed cases have high rebound potential. Supracrestal fiberotomy can be considered for severe rotations, but the cornerstone is indefinite retention and patient ownership of compliance. Failure to plan robust retention is a common cause of post-aligner relapse and dissatisfaction.

title: Post-Orthognathic Class III — Relapse Risk & Retention Protocol
short: 24M • 14 months post BSSO + Le Fort I • early anterior relapse

patient.medical_history: Healthy. Underwent two-jaw surgery (Le Fort I advancement + BSSO setback) 14 months ago for skeletal Class III. Finishing orthodontics completed 6 months ago.
patient.chief_complaint: My lower teeth are starting to sit ahead of the upper teeth again and the bite feels off.

clinical_findings.radiographs: Current ceph shows 1.5–2 mm anterior relapse of mandibular position relative to immediate post-surgical records; condyles seated; no hardware failure.

guidelines: Class III relapse patterns and timing

vignette.demographics: 24-year-old male, 14 months after bimaxillary surgery for skeletal Class III, orthodontic finishing completed 6 months previously.
vignette.chief: Subjective and objective return of anterior crossbite tendency.
vignette.clinical: Edge-to-edge to 1 mm reverse overjet developing, posterior occlusion mildly shifting, no pain or limitation of opening.
vignette.radio: Cephalometric comparison demonstrates modest anterior relapse of the mandible; condyles remain seated in fossae; fixation hardware intact.

questions.q: What is the most likely primary contributor to this early skeletal relapse pattern?
options: Patient non-compliance with elastics alone
Condylar resorption or hardware failure
Inherent tendency of Class III surgical corrections to show some anterior relapse, especially if soft-tissue and muscular adaptation are incomplete
Orthodontic finishing was too perfect
questions.explanation: Class III corrections (particularly mandibular setback) have a well-documented tendency for some anterior relapse related to soft-tissue stretch, muscular adaptation, and residual growth or remodeling. Condylar resorption and hardware failure are less common but must be ruled out; the vignette indicates seated condyles and intact fixation.

questions.q: The most appropriate immediate management is:
options: Return to surgery for re-operation

Re-institute inter-arch elastics or limited fixed appliances under close surgical-orthodontic supervision while quantifying the relapse; discuss possible compensatory orthodontics versus revision surgery
Ignore the change because some relapse is normal
Extract lower premolars immediately
questions.explanation: Early detection allows an attempt at dental compensation or guidance of the residual shift with elastics or limited appliances while the surgical team evaluates whether the relapse is progressive. Immediate re-operation is rarely indicated for modest early change; watchful interdisciplinary management is the standard first step.

questions.q: Red-team long-term retention principle after Class III orthognathic surgery:
options: Retention can be discontinued after 12 months
Prolonged (often indefinite) retention with both fixed and removable components, combined with periodic surgical-orthodontic review, is required because late relapse can continue for several years
Only a Hawley retainer is needed
Retention is unnecessary once hardware is removed
questions.explanation: Skeletal Class III patients remain at elevated risk for late relapse for several years post-surgery. Indefinite retention strategies and scheduled interdisciplinary follow-up are considered standard of care to protect both the occlusal result and the investment of surgery.

title: Acute Closed Lock — Sudden Cessation of Clicking with Limited Opening
short: 28F • 2-year reciprocal click → sudden lock 4 days ago • Max opening 27 mm

patient.medical_history: Healthy, no medications, occasional gum chewing, history of nighttime clenching reported by partner.
patient.chief_complaint: My right jaw used to click for years. Four days ago the click stopped and now I can barely open my mouth. It hurts to try.

clinical_findings.mobility: Maximum unassisted opening 27 mm with deflection to the right; passive stretch to 31 mm with hard end-feel; contralateral excursions limited; right TMJ load test positive.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Panoramic unremarkable; CBCT (if obtained) shows normal cortical contours, reduced translation of right condyle on open mouth view.

flags: Sudden loss of previous reciprocal click
Limited opening <40 mm with ipsilateral deflection
guidelines: AAOP Guidelines for Assessment and Management of TMD

vignette.demographics: 28-year-old healthy female, no systemic disease, reports chronic gum chewing and nocturnal clenching.
vignette.chief: Right TMJ reciprocal clicking for ~2 years. Four days ago clicking abruptly ceased; progressive limitation of opening and right-sided pain on attempted wide opening or chewing.
vignette.clinical: Unassisted maximum opening 27 mm with deflection to the ipsilateral (right) side. Passive stretch reaches 31 mm with hard end-feel. Right joint loading produces familiar pain. No muscle trigger points of primary significance. Cranial nerves intact. No occlusal step or trauma history.
vignette.endo: All teeth vital, no odontogenic source.
vignette.radio: Panoramic normal bony contours. Open-mouth CBCT (when indicated) demonstrates limited translation of the right condyle consistent with mechanical obstruction.

questions.q: According to DC/TMD Axis I criteria, what is the most accurate primary joint diagnosis for the right TMJ?
options: Disc displacement with reduction with intermittent locking
Disc displacement without reduction with limited opening
Degenerative joint disease (osteoarthritis)
Subluxation / hypermobility
questions.explanation: DC/TMD requires history of prior click that stopped, accompanied by limited opening (<40 mm) and ipsilateral deflection for the diagnosis of disc displacement without reduction with limited opening (closed lock). Intermittent locking still allows reduction. DJD requires crepitus + radiographic bony change. Subluxation is characterized by open lock / hypermobility, the opposite presentation.

questions.q: First-line evidence-based management for this acute closed-lock presentation (no red-flag systemic features) is:
options: Immediate arthrocentesis or arthroscopy under general anesthesia
Education, soft diet, NSAIDs, jaw exercises / self-mobilization, and short-term occlusal appliance as needed; most acute locks improve conservatively
Mandatory MRI before any treatment is started
Irreversible occlusal adjustment or full-mouth reconstruction to 'unlock' the joint
questions.explanation: AAOP and DC/TMD-aligned care pathways emphasize conservative, reversible therapy first for acute disc displacement without reduction. The majority of patients regain functional opening with education, anti-inflammatory measures, and guided self-mobilization. Imaging is reserved for non-responders or atypical features. Irreversible dental changes are contraindicated as initial therapy.

questions.q: Red-team decision point: Which finding would most strongly prompt earlier advanced imaging or specialist referral rather than a pure conservative trial?
options: Mild ipsilateral masseter tenderness
Progressive neurologic signs, sudden sensory change in V3 distribution, or constitutional symptoms suggesting secondary (neoplastic / systemic) disease
Patient anxiety about the click history
Desire for a rapid return to wide opening for aesthetic reasons only
questions.explanation: Red flags (neurologic deficit, progressive sensory change, weight loss, night pain, history of malignancy) mandate prompt imaging and medical work-up to exclude secondary TMD or intracranial / neoplastic sources. Ordinary myalgia or patient preference alone does not justify early invasive escalation.

title: Chronic Myofascial Pain with Elevated Axis II Psychosocial Load
short: 42F • Bilateral masseter/temporalis pain 14 months • High PHQ-9 / GCPS

patient.medical_history: Generalized anxiety disorder, insomnia, remote history of depression; currently on sertraline 75 mg. High job stress.
patient.chief_complaint: Constant dull ache in both cheeks and temples for over a year. Worse with stress and at the end of the day. Clicking is occasional but not the main problem.

clinical_findings.mobility: Opening 44 mm without restriction; familiar pain on palpation of bilateral masseter and temporalis; multiple active trigger points with referral to teeth and temple; no joint sounds of clinical significance today.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Panoramic normal; no indication for CBCT at this stage.

flags: Multiple active trigger points with referral

vignette.demographics: 42-year-old female with anxiety, insomnia, and high occupational stress on SSRI.
vignette.chief: Bilateral facial and temporal aching pain for 14 months, fluctuating with stress, sleep, and work demands. Occasional non-painful click.
vignette.clinical: Normal range of motion. Familiar pain reproduced by palpation of masseter and temporalis at multiple sites; clear referral patterns to maxillary teeth and temple. Joint loading non-contributory. Occlusion stable. No mucosal or dental pathology explaining the pain.
vignette.endo: All teeth respond normally within normal limits; no odontogenic source.
vignette.radio: Panoramic unremarkable; advanced imaging not indicated as first step.

questions.q: In the DC/TMD framework, which statement best characterizes this patient’s diagnostic profile?
options: Pure Axis I joint disorder requiring surgical consideration
Axis I myofascial pain with referral plus clinically significant Axis II psychosocial contribution that must be addressed for successful outcome
Primary degenerative joint disease
Acute closed lock
questions.explanation: DC/TMD explicitly separates Axis I (physical diagnosis — here myofascial pain with referral) from Axis II (pain-related disability, depression, anxiety, jaw functional limitation). High psychosocial load predicts poorer response to purely biomedical interventions and requires concurrent behavioral / psychological strategies.

questions.q: Most appropriate initial treatment strategy consistent with current AAOP / dual-axis principles is:
options: Immediate long-term opioid or high-dose muscle relaxant therapy

Education, self-care, sleep hygiene, brief CBT or pain psychology referral, physical therapy / self-mobilization, and short-term pharmacologic support (NSAID or low-dose TCA/muscle relaxant) as needed
Irreversible occlusal equilibration as the primary intervention
Arthrocentesis of both TMJs
questions.explanation: Evidence-based care for chronic myofascial pain with elevated Axis II scores prioritizes reversible, multimodal approaches that address both the physical and psychosocial domains. Occlusal adjustment as primary therapy lacks support and risks iatrogenic harm. Surgery is not indicated for myofascial pain.

questions.q: Red-team pitfall: What is the most common error that prolongs disability in this presentation?
options: Providing patient education about the benign nature of most TMD
Repeatedly escalating irreversible dental or surgical interventions while ignoring the Axis II contribution and sleep/stress factors
Screening for depression and anxiety
Using a short-term stabilization appliance as an adjunct
questions.explanation: A classic failure mode is exclusive focus on peripheral dental or joint 'corrections' while the central and psychosocial drivers remain unaddressed. This leads to treatment-seeking cycles, increased disability, and potential iatrogenic damage. Dual-axis management from the outset reduces this risk.

title: TMJ Degenerative Joint Disease with Crepitus and Functional Limitation
short: 58F • Long-standing crepitus • Progressive opening reduction • Osteophyte on CBCT

patient.medical_history: Osteoarthritis of knees and hands, BMI 31, postmenopausal, no bisphosphonates.
patient.chief_complaint: My right jaw has ground and cracked for years. Lately it feels stiffer and I can’t open as wide. Pain is moderate but constant when chewing.

clinical_findings.mobility: Maximum opening 34 mm with deflection; coarse crepitus on right TMJ auscultation/palpation; familiar pain on loading; mild masseter co-activation.
clinical_findings.radiographs: CBCT demonstrates right condylar flattening, osteophyte formation, and subchondral sclerosis consistent with degenerative joint disease.

guidelines: DC/TMD criteria for Degenerative Joint Disease

vignette.demographics: 58-year-old postmenopausal female with polyarticular osteoarthritis.
vignette.chief: Long-standing right TMJ grinding/crepitus with recent reduction in opening and load-related pain.
vignette.clinical: Opening 34 mm, ipsilateral deflection, palpable coarse crepitus, positive right joint loading. No acute closed-lock history. Mild secondary myalgia.
vignette.endo: Dentition stable; no acute dental pathology.
vignette.radio: CBCT confirms degenerative changes (flattening, osteophyte, sclerosis) of the right condyle; left side milder.

questions.q: DC/TMD diagnosis that best fits the combination of crepitus and positive CBCT bony changes is:
options: Disc displacement with reduction
Degenerative joint disease (osteoarthritis) of the TMJ
Myofascial pain only
Acute traumatic arthritis
questions.explanation: DC/TMD defines Degenerative Joint Disease when clinical crepitus (or imaging evidence of bony change) is present. Disc displacement diagnoses do not require bony change. Pure myofascial pain lacks joint sounds and radiographic findings of this type.

questions.q: Most appropriate next management step after confirmation of DJD in a patient with moderate pain and functional limitation is:
options: Immediate total joint replacement
Conservative care (education, soft diet, NSAIDs or topical agents, physical therapy, stabilization appliance) with reassessment; escalate to arthrocentesis or other interventions only if refractory
Long-term high-dose systemic corticosteroids
Extraction of all remaining molars to 'unload' the joint
questions.explanation: Even with radiographic DJD, the majority of patients are managed successfully with conservative measures. Interventional procedures (arthrocentesis, arthroscopy, open surgery) are reserved for persistent pain/disability after an adequate conservative trial. Total joint replacement is a last resort for end-stage disease with severe dysfunction.

questions.q: Which statement regarding imaging in suspected TMJ DJD is most accurate?
options: Panoramic radiography alone is always sufficient for definitive diagnosis
CBCT is the modality of choice for evaluating osseous changes; MRI is preferred when disc position or soft-tissue detail is the primary question
Imaging is never useful once crepitus is heard
Bone scan is required in every case before treatment
questions.explanation: CBCT provides high-resolution assessment of cortical and subchondral bone and is preferred for osseous DJD evaluation. MRI remains superior for disc position, effusion, and soft-tissue detail. Imaging decisions are driven by whether the findings will change management.

title: Burning Mouth Syndrome — Primary vs Secondary Work-up
short: 61F • Daily burning of tongue/palate 9 months • Normal mucosa • Dry mouth symptoms

patient.medical_history: Type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.4 %), hypothyroidism on levothyroxine, postmenopausal, on ACE inhibitor; reports dry mouth and altered taste.
patient.chief_complaint: My tongue and the roof of my mouth burn every day, especially in the afternoon. Nothing looks wrong but it is driving me crazy.

clinical_findings.mobility: Oral mucosa appears normal; no erythema, ulceration, or white patches; unstimulated salivary flow reduced; taste testing subtle dysgeusia.
clinical_findings.radiographs: No relevant findings; panoramic normal.

flags: Must exclude secondary causes before primary BMS label
guidelines: IHS / IASP criteria for Burning Mouth Syndrome
AAOM position on secondary burning mouth evaluation

vignette.demographics: 61-year-old postmenopausal female with T2DM, hypothyroidism, and ACE-inhibitor use.
vignette.chief: Persistent daily burning of tongue and hard palate for 9 months, worse later in the day, accompanied by dry mouth and mild taste change. No visible lesions according to patient.
vignette.clinical: Mucosa of normal color and texture. Reduced unstimulated salivary flow. No candidal plaques, no lichenoid striae, no ulceration. Cranial nerves intact. Dentition and prostheses non-contributory.
vignette.radio: No odontogenic or bony pathology explaining symptoms.

questions.q: Before assigning a diagnosis of primary (idiopathic) Burning Mouth Syndrome, which step is essential?
options: Immediate long-term systemic clonazepam without further testing
Systematic exclusion of secondary causes (medications, xerostomia, candidiasis, nutritional deficiency, endocrine disease, mucosal disease, parafunction)
Extraction of all remaining teeth
Mandatory brain MRI in every case
questions.explanation: Primary BMS is a diagnosis of exclusion. Current AAOM and IASP-aligned approaches require evaluation for secondary drivers (drug-induced xerostomia, candidiasis, iron/B12/folate deficiency, uncontrolled diabetes, thyroid dysfunction, contact reactions, etc.). Treating as primary without this work-up risks missing reversible causes.

questions.q: In this patient, which factor is most likely contributing as a secondary driver of oral burning?
options: Occasional gum chewing alone
Polypharmacy (ACE inhibitor) + diabetic and thyroid disease + reduced salivary flow
A single asymptomatic restoration
Normal aging with no other factors
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors are well-documented contributors to burning and dysgeusia. Uncontrolled or borderline diabetes, hypothyroidism, and hyposalivation further lower the threshold for oral sensory symptoms. Addressing these systemic and medication factors is part of first-line management.

questions.q: If secondary causes are optimized and burning persists, which pharmacologic approach has the strongest evidence as first-line for primary BMS?
options: Long-term high-dose opioids
Topical clonazepam (suck-and-spit) or low-dose systemic neuromodulators (clonazepam, alpha-lipoic acid, or selected antidepressants) with realistic expectation setting
Broad-spectrum antibiotics for 6 weeks
Systemic corticosteroids indefinitely
questions.explanation: Evidence supports topical clonazepam and certain systemic neuromodulators for primary BMS. Opioids, antibiotics, and chronic steroids lack efficacy and carry substantial risk. Patient education about the neuropathic nature of the condition is equally important.

title: Trigeminal Neuralgia vs Persistent Idiopathic Dentoalveolar Pain
short: 67F • Lancinating right V2 pain • Trigger zones • Multiple endodontically treated teeth

patient.medical_history: Hypertension, no MS, no prior stroke; several root-canal-treated maxillary teeth on the right.
patient.chief_complaint: Electric-shock stabs of pain in my right upper jaw and cheek. Light touch or cold air sets it off. Dentists have done three root canals but the pain keeps coming back in waves.

clinical_findings.mobility: Sharp, brief, electric pain triggered by light touch in right V2 skin and alveolar mucosa; refractory period after attacks; no continuous background ache between paroxysms; treated teeth non-tender to percussion.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Multiple RCT teeth without residual periapical radiolucency; no osseous pathology.

flags: Classic TN phenotype vs continuous dentoalveolar pain
guidelines: IHS International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD-3) for Trigeminal Neuralgia
IASP criteria for Persistent Idiopathic Dentoalveolar Pain (formerly atypical odontalgia)

vignette.demographics: 67-year-old hypertensive female with multiple prior endodontic procedures on the right maxilla.
vignette.chief: Severe, brief, electric-shock-like pain in right V2 distribution triggered by light touch, talking, or cold air. Attacks last seconds; patient is pain-free between them. Several root canals performed without lasting relief.
vignette.clinical: Trigger zones on right cheek and alveolar mucosa. No continuous dull ache. Percussion and palpation of treated teeth do not reproduce the electric pain. Neurologic exam otherwise normal.
vignette.endo: Previously treated teeth show no residual infection or fracture on clinical and radiographic exam.
vignette.radio: No periapical or osseous lesions explaining the paroxysmal pain.

questions.q: The history of strictly paroxysmal, triggerable, electric pain with refractory periods and pain-free intervals is most consistent with:
options: Persistent idiopathic dentoalveolar pain (continuous background ache)
Classical trigeminal neuralgia (ICHD-3)
Chronic myofascial pain with referral
Acute apical periodontitis
questions.explanation: Classical trigeminal neuralgia is defined by recurrent, unilateral, brief, electric shock-like pains with abrupt onset and termination, triggered by innocuous stimuli, and often followed by a refractory period. Persistent idiopathic dentoalveolar pain is continuous or near-continuous and lacks the classic paroxysmal electric quality.

questions.q: Most appropriate next diagnostic / management step after recognizing the TN phenotype is:
options: Another round of endodontic retreatment or extraction of the previously treated teeth

Neurologic evaluation, MRI (to exclude secondary causes), and initiation of first-line pharmacotherapy (carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine) with dental procedures withheld unless clear odontogenic pathology exists
Immediate Gamma-knife radiosurgery
Long-term opioid therapy as monotherapy
questions.explanation: Once the clinical diagnosis of TN is made, guidelines recommend MRI to exclude secondary causes (MS, tumor, vascular compression detailed assessment) and prompt trial of first-line sodium-channel blockers. Further irreversible dental treatment in the absence of clear local pathology is a common source of morbidity and does not address the neuropathic mechanism.

questions.q: Red-team lesson from this case: What is the principal risk of repeatedly attributing classic TN pain to 'failed' root-canal teeth?
options: Slight delay in starting carbamazepine
Unnecessary irreversible dental procedures, delayed correct diagnosis, and potential worsening of the pain condition or legal exposure
Patient satisfaction with continued dental visits
Improved salivary flow
questions.explanation: A major source of iatrogenic harm in orofacial pain is the repeated performance of endodontic or surgical procedures on teeth that are not the true source of a neuropathic pain disorder. Early recognition of the TN phenotype and appropriate medical referral protects the patient and the clinician.

title: Symptomatic Oral Lichen Planus with Erosive Component — Pain and Malignancy Surveillance
short: 54F • Bilateral buccal burning & sensitivity 11 months • Reticular + erosive lesions

patient.medical_history: Hypertension, no hepatitis C, no medications strongly associated with lichenoid reactions; never-smoker.
patient.chief_complaint: The insides of my cheeks burn and feel raw, especially when I eat spicy or acidic food. It has been going on for almost a year.

clinical_findings.mobility: Bilateral buccal mucosa shows white reticular striae (Wickham) with areas of erythema and shallow erosion; mild desquamative changes on gingiva; no indurated ulcers or lymphadenopathy.
clinical_findings.radiographs: N/A

flags: Need to confirm diagnosis histologically when erosive
guidelines: AAOM / WHO criteria for oral lichen planus
Malignant transformation risk and biopsy thresholds

vignette.demographics: 54-year-old female, non-smoker, no known hepatitis C or lichenoid drug exposure.
vignette.chief: Bilateral buccal mucosal burning and sensitivity to spicy/acidic foods for 11 months.
vignette.clinical: Classic bilateral white reticular striae with interspersed erythematous and shallow erosive areas on buccal mucosa; mild desquamative gingivitis. No solitary indurated ulcer, no cervical lymphadenopathy, no cutaneous lesions currently.
vignette.radio: N/A — soft-tissue diagnosis.

questions.q: Most appropriate next step when erosive oral lichen planus is clinically suspected is:
options: Empiric high-potency topical steroid indefinitely without tissue diagnosis
Incisional biopsy of representative erosive/reticular tissue (and consideration of direct immunofluorescence if needed) to confirm diagnosis and exclude dysplasia or other immune-mediated disease
Immediate systemic chemotherapy
Extraction of adjacent teeth
questions.explanation: Histopathologic confirmation is recommended, especially for erosive disease, both to support the diagnosis of OLP and to exclude dysplasia, carcinoma, or other vesiculobullous disorders. Empiric long-term steroids without diagnosis are discouraged.

questions.q: First-line therapy for symptomatic erosive oral lichen planus after confirmation is typically:
options: Long-term systemic corticosteroids as monotherapy

High-potency topical corticosteroids (e.g., clobetasol or fluocinonide in adhesive base or gel) with or without topical calcineurin inhibitors, plus elimination of local irritants and candidal prophylaxis when indicated
Systemic antifungals alone
Radiation therapy
questions.explanation: Topical high-potency corticosteroids remain the mainstay for symptomatic erosive OLP. Systemic steroids are reserved for severe, refractory, or multi-site disease. Adjunctive measures (irritant removal, antifungal coverage when using potent steroids) improve outcomes and reduce complications.

questions.q: Red-team surveillance point: What is the most important long-term responsibility after diagnosing oral lichen planus?
options: Reassure the patient that no follow-up is ever needed
Periodic clinical surveillance for malignant transformation (higher risk with erosive / atrophic forms) and prompt biopsy of any non-healing, indurated, or suspicious change
Annual full-mouth radiographic series solely for the lichen planus
Lifelong systemic immunosuppression in all patients
questions.explanation: Oral lichen planus carries a small but real risk of malignant transformation, particularly in erosive and atrophic forms. Structured long-term mucosal surveillance and a low threshold for re-biopsy of changing or non-healing sites are essential components of care and risk management.

title: Moderate OSA in a CPAP-intolerant patient — MAD candidacy & titration
short: 48M • BMI 31 • AHI 22 • CPAP intolerance • Dentate

patient.medical_history: Hypertension (controlled on lisinopril), GERD, BMI 31. No cardiac disease. Epworth Sleepiness Scale 14. PSG: AHI 22 (supine 31), lowest SpO2 84%. Tried CPAP 4 months — claustrophobia and mask leaks; average nightly use <2 h.
patient.chief_complaint: I can’t tolerate the CPAP machine. My doctor said a dental appliance might help. I snore loudly and my wife says I stop breathing.

clinical_findings.mobility: Full dentition, Class I occlusion, mild lower anterior crowding, 2 mm overjet.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Panoramic: adequate bone levels, no pathology. Lateral cephalogram: mild retrognathia, elongated soft palate.

guidelines: AADSM/AASM Clinical Practice Guideline for Oral Appliance Therapy (2015, updated consensus)

vignette.demographics: 48 y/o Male, BMI 31, controlled HTN, GERD, ESS 14.
vignette.chief: CPAP intolerance; seeks oral appliance therapy for moderate OSA.
vignette.clinical: Dentate, Class I, mild crowding, healthy periodontium, 2 mm overjet. No TMD history.
vignette.radio: Panoramic normal; cephalometric mild retrognathia + elongated soft palate.

questions.q: According to current AADSM/AASM guidance, which statement best supports offering a custom-fabricated mandibular advancement device (MAD) to this patient?
options: MAD is first-line only for mild OSA; moderate OSA requires CPAP or surgery
Custom MAD is an appropriate alternative for adult patients with moderate OSA who are intolerant of or refuse CPAP
Only thermoplastic boil-and-bite appliances are indicated at AHI 22
MAD is contraindicated once AHI exceeds 15
questions.explanation: AADSM/AASM guidelines support custom MAD as primary therapy for mild OSA and as an alternative for moderate OSA (and selected severe cases) when the patient is CPAP-intolerant or refuses CPAP. Boil-and-bite devices are not recommended for long-term management. AHI 22 falls squarely in the moderate range where MAD is evidence-based.

questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step after delivery of a custom MAD?
options: Immediate maximum protrusion and discharge
Gradual titration of advancement guided by subjective symptoms and, when possible, objective follow-up (HSAT or PSG) to verify residual AHI and SpO2
No follow-up needed if the patient reports better sleep
Mandatory multi-piece maxillary expansion first
questions.explanation: Best practice is incremental titration (typically 0.5–1 mm increments) while monitoring symptoms, occlusion, and TMJ status. Objective verification (HSAT or PSG) is preferred, especially in moderate–severe disease or when residual symptoms persist, to confirm therapeutic efficacy and detect incomplete response.

questions.q: Red-team risk point: Which dental/occlusal change is most frequently observed with long-term MAD use and must be disclosed during informed consent?
options: Irreversible posterior open bite in every patient
Forward movement of mandibular incisors, retroclination of maxillary incisors, and reduction of overjet/overbite; bite changes may persist after appliance cessation
No occlusal changes ever occur with custom devices
Only temporary muscle soreness with no dental side effects
questions.explanation: Longitudinal studies show measurable dental side effects (mandibular incisor proclination, maxillary incisor retroclination, decreased overjet/overbite, and occasional posterior open bite). These changes can be permanent. Informed consent must include discussion of occlusal changes, morning occlusal exercises, and periodic monitoring.

title: Severe OSA + edentulous mandible — appliance options & referral thresholds
short: 62M • AHI 41 • Edentulous mandible • CPAP failure

patient.medical_history: BMI 34, atrial fibrillation (anticoagulated), type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.4%), ESS 16. PSG: AHI 41, ODI 38, nadir SpO2 76%. CPAP tried — poor adherence due to pressure intolerance and nasal obstruction.
patient.chief_complaint: I need something other than the CPAP. I have no lower teeth and a partial upper.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: Maxillary partial denture; residual ridge moderate resorption.
clinical_findings.mobility: Edentulous mandible, moderate atrophy; opposing maxillary Kennedy Class I RPD.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Panoramic: severe mandibular residual ridge resorption, mental foramina near crest.

guidelines: AADSM guidelines on oral appliances in edentulous patients
ITI / prosthodontic considerations for implant-retained appliances

vignette.demographics: 62 y/o Male, BMI 34, AFib on anticoagulation, T2DM, ESS 16, AHI 41.
vignette.chief: Severe OSA, CPAP failure, seeks alternative; edentulous mandible.
vignette.clinical: Edentulous mandible with moderate atrophy; maxillary RPD. No active TMD.
vignette.radio: Panoramic shows advanced mandibular ridge resorption.

questions.q: In an edentulous patient with severe OSA, which statement best reflects current evidence-based options?
options: No oral appliance is possible once the patient is edentulous
Implant-retained mandibular advancement prosthesis or tongue-retaining device may be considered; traditional tooth-borne MAD is not feasible
Only surgical maxillomandibular advancement is indicated
A conventional complete denture alone will reliably treat AHI 41
questions.explanation: Tooth-borne MADs require adequate dentition or stable implants. In fully edentulous patients, options include implant-retained advancement prostheses or tongue-retaining devices (TRDs). Conventional dentures alone do not provide reliable mandibular advancement. Surgical options remain for selected non-responders after medical optimization.

questions.q: Given AHI 41, cardiovascular comorbidity, and CPAP failure, what is the most appropriate initial interdisciplinary step?
options: Fabricate a temporary boil-and-bite appliance and reassess in 12 months
Coordinate with sleep medicine for optimized CPAP re-trial (pressure relief, different interface, humidification) while simultaneously evaluating surgical or implant-retained options
Immediate MMA surgery without further medical input
No further therapy is indicated once CPAP is refused
questions.explanation: Severe OSA with cardiac comorbidity warrants aggressive residual-disease reduction. A structured re-challenge of CPAP with modern interfaces/pressure-relief algorithms is still first-line; concurrent evaluation for implant-retained appliances or surgical consultation (ENT/OMFS) is appropriate when adherence remains poor.

questions.q: Red-team point: Why is a conventional soft-liner or temporary denture-based advancement device generally discouraged for long-term management of severe OSA?
options: They are too expensive
