Insufficient retention, unpredictable titration, rapid loss of protrusion, and inability to maintain therapeutic advancement under sleep forces
They always cause implant failure
They are recommended as first-line by AADSM
questions.explanation: Temporary or soft-liner devices lack the rigidity and retention needed for consistent mandibular advancement throughout the night. They lose protrusion quickly and cannot be reliably titrated or verified objectively — unacceptable in severe OSA with cardiovascular risk.

title: MAD side effects — posterior open bite & management algorithm
short: 55F • AHI 18 • 3-year MAD use • Progressive open bite

patient.medical_history: Moderate OSA diagnosed 3 years ago (AHI 18). Custom MAD used nightly with good adherence and ESS improvement (from 12 to 5). Recent dental exam notes progressive anterior open bite and posterior occlusal changes. No TMD pain.
patient.chief_complaint: My bite has changed — my front teeth don’t touch anymore and food gets stuck in the back.

clinical_findings.mobility: Anterior open bite 2.5 mm; reduced overjet; posterior teeth in infra-occlusion bilaterally; mild mesial drift of molars.
clinical_findings.radiographs: No root resorption; bone levels normal.

guidelines: AADSM consensus on dental side effects of oral appliances
Longitudinal studies of occlusal changes with MAD

vignette.demographics: 55 y/o Female, moderate OSA controlled with MAD for 3 years.
vignette.chief: Progressive anterior open bite and posterior occlusal changes after long-term MAD use.
vignette.clinical: 2.5 mm anterior open bite, reduced overjet, bilateral posterior infra-occlusion; no pain or TMD signs.
vignette.radio: No root resorption or periodontal bone loss.

questions.q: What is the most evidence-based first management step for progressive posterior open bite in a patient whose OSA remains well controlled by MAD?
options: Immediate permanent cessation of the MAD and acceptance of residual OSA
Temporary reduction or cessation of advancement, institution of morning occlusal exercises / jaw-stretching protocol, and close monitoring of both occlusion and OSA control
Immediate full-mouth orthodontic re-treatment while continuing full protrusion
Conversion to a tongue-retaining device only
questions.explanation: When occlusal changes appear, the first step is usually to reduce or temporarily stop advancement, institute daily morning occlusal recovery exercises (chewing, biting on a soft wafer, or guided protrusion/retrusion), and re-evaluate both the bite and residual AHI. Abrupt permanent cessation risks return of uncontrolled OSA; orthodontics is reserved for persistent, functionally significant changes after conservative measures.

questions.q: Which statement about the permanence of MAD-related occlusal changes is most accurate?
options: All occlusal changes reverse completely within 4 weeks of stopping the appliance
Some dental movements (especially incisor inclination and overjet reduction) may persist even after appliance discontinuation
Posterior open bite never occurs with custom-titrated devices
Only skeletal changes occur; teeth never move
questions.explanation: Longitudinal data show that while muscle and some soft-tissue adaptation can recover, dental tipping and arch-form changes are often only partially reversible. Informed consent and periodic occlusal monitoring are therefore mandatory.

questions.q: Red-team consent point: Which additional risk should be explicitly discussed when a patient develops clinically significant open bite while on MAD therapy?
options: That the open bite will always self-correct without intervention

Possible need for future orthodontic or restorative correction, potential impact on masticatory function, and the trade-off between continuing MAD (OSA control) versus modifying or stopping it (bite recovery)
That surgery is required in every case
No further discussion is needed once the appliance is delivered
questions.explanation: Patients must understand the risk–benefit balance: continued MAD use may maintain OSA control at the cost of progressive occlusal change that could later require orthodontics or restorative treatment. Shared decision-making and documentation are essential.

title: Pediatric OSA + orthodontic growth modification considerations
short: 9M • AHI 7.2 • Adenotonsillar hypertrophy • Narrow maxilla

patient.medical_history: Habitual snoring, witnessed apneas, restless sleep, daytime inattention. PSG: AHI 7.2 (obstructive), nadir SpO2 88%. ENT notes 3+ tonsils and adenoid hypertrophy. Orthodontic exam: narrow maxilla, bilateral crossbite tendency, high-arched palate.
patient.chief_complaint: Pediatrician and ENT are discussing tonsillectomy; parents also ask about expansion to help the airway.

clinical_findings.mobility: Maxillary constriction, high palate, mild crowding; no active caries.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Panoramic age-appropriate; lateral ceph shows reduced airway and adenoid pad.

guidelines: AAO considerations for rapid maxillary expansion in OSA
ENT adenotonsillectomy as first-line in appropriate candidates

vignette.demographics: 9 y/o Male with habitual snoring, AHI 7.2, adenotonsillar hypertrophy, maxillary constriction.
vignette.chief: Parents seeking both surgical and orthodontic airway options.
vignette.clinical: Narrow maxilla, high palate, mixed dentition, 3+ tonsils.
vignette.radio: Ceph shows reduced pharyngeal airway and adenoid hypertrophy.

questions.q: According to current pediatric OSA guidelines, what is the most appropriate first-line treatment for this child with moderate adenotonsillar hypertrophy and AHI 7.2?
options: Immediate rapid maxillary expansion alone
Adenotonsillectomy as first-line surgical therapy in most children with OSA and adenotonsillar hypertrophy, with orthodontic expansion considered adjunctively or for residual disease
Lifelong CPAP as the only evidence-based option
Observation only until skeletal maturity
questions.explanation: AAP and AASM guidelines identify adenotonsillectomy as first-line treatment for most children with OSA and significant adenotonsillar hypertrophy. Rapid maxillary expansion (RME) can improve nasal airway and may help residual or mild OSA, especially with transverse deficiency, but is generally adjunctive rather than primary when large tonsils/adenoids are present.

questions.q: When is rapid maxillary expansion most reasonably considered in the pediatric OSA pathway?
options: Only after the patient is fully grown
As an adjunct in children with transverse maxillary deficiency, nasal obstruction, or residual OSA after adenotonsillectomy; not as a routine replacement for indicated T&A
As mandatory treatment before any ENT referral
Never; expansion has no airway effect
questions.explanation: Evidence supports RME for improving nasal airflow and reducing AHI in selected children with constricted maxillae. It is best timed when the midpalatal suture is still responsive and is coordinated with ENT management rather than used in isolation when large adenoids/tonsils dominate the obstruction.

questions.q: Red-team point: What is the principal risk of delaying indicated adenotonsillectomy while pursuing only orthodontic expansion in a symptomatic child with AHI 7.2?
options: No risk; expansion always cures pediatric OSA
Continued intermittent hypoxia, neurocognitive and behavioral sequelae, and possible progression of disease while waiting for dental results
Only mild temporary snoring
Guaranteed need for future MMA surgery
questions.explanation: Pediatric OSA is associated with measurable neurobehavioral, cardiovascular, and growth effects. Delaying proven first-line therapy (T&A when indicated) while awaiting the slower effects of expansion risks ongoing hypoxic burden and developmental impact.

title: Combination therapy & residual AHI after MAD
short: 51M • Baseline AHI 28 • MAD residual AHI 14 • Persistent sleepiness

patient.medical_history: Baseline AHI 28, BMI 29. Custom MAD titrated to maximum comfortable protrusion. Follow-up HSAT with appliance: residual AHI 14, ESS still 11. Patient refuses return to CPAP.
patient.chief_complaint: I feel better than with nothing, but I’m still tired and my wife says I still snore some nights.

clinical_findings.mobility: MAD in place; mild tooth mobility of lower anteriors noted after 14 months of use.
clinical_findings.radiographs: No significant root resorption.

flags: Need for combination or alternative strategies
guidelines: AADSM guidance on incomplete response to oral appliances

vignette.demographics: 51 y/o Male, baseline AHI 28 → residual AHI 14 on MAD, persistent ESS 11.
vignette.chief: Incomplete symptomatic and objective response to optimally titrated MAD.
vignette.clinical: Well-fitting MAD, mild lower anterior mobility, no active TMD.
vignette.radio: No root resorption.

questions.q: What is the most appropriate next management step for residual moderate OSA and persistent sleepiness despite a titrated MAD?
options: Declare treatment complete because any reduction in AHI is sufficient
Discuss combination therapy (MAD + positional therapy, weight loss, or limited CPAP use), further titration if possible, or referral for alternative medical/surgical options
Immediately extract teeth to allow a larger appliance
No further investigation is indicated
questions.explanation: Residual AHI ≥10–15 with persistent symptoms constitutes incomplete response. Options include combination approaches (positional therapy, weight management, hybrid MAD+CPAP for part of the night), verification of titration limits, or referral back to sleep medicine/ENT/OMFS for additional modalities.

questions.q: Which objective finding most strongly supports the need for additional therapy beyond the current MAD?
options: Subjective improvement alone is always enough
Residual AHI 14 + ESS 11 indicating ongoing clinically significant disease burden
Any residual snoring regardless of AHI
Mild tooth mobility alone
questions.explanation: Both objective (residual AHI) and subjective (ESS) residual disease justify escalation or combination therapy. Mild tooth mobility is a side-effect monitoring issue but is not the primary driver for changing OSA therapy.

questions.q: Red-team point: Why is simply increasing MAD protrusion to the absolute maximum without regard to joint or occlusal tolerance potentially harmful?
options: It has no downside
Risk of accelerating occlusal change, precipitating TMD symptoms, reducing long-term adherence, and still failing to normalize AHI if the residual obstruction is positional or multilevel
It always cures residual AHI
It is required by AADSM titration protocols
questions.explanation: Over-advancement beyond comfort increases dental side effects and TMD risk while adherence often falls. Residual obstruction may also be multilevel or positional and therefore not fully correctable by further mandibular advancement alone.

title: Pre-surgical dental evaluation for maxillomandibular advancement (MMA)
short: 38M • AHI 52 • CPAP failure • Considering MMA

patient.medical_history: Severe OSA (AHI 52), BMI 27, failed CPAP and MAD (residual AHI 24). ENT and OMFS evaluating maxillomandibular advancement. Class II skeletal pattern, 6 mm overjet, healthy dentition.
patient.chief_complaint: I’m being worked up for jaw-advancement surgery. What does the dentist need to check first?

clinical_findings.mobility: Class II Division 1, 6 mm overjet, mild crowding lower anterior, third molars present.
clinical_findings.radiographs: CBCT: adequate bone, third molars impacted; airway volume reduced.

flags: Severe OSA refractory to non-surgical therapy
Need for comprehensive pre-surgical dental clearance
guidelines: AAOMS / sleep-surgery consensus on MMA for OSA
Pre-surgical dental and periodontal clearance principles
AADSM role in perioperative oral-appliance bridging

vignette.demographics: 38 y/o Male, AHI 52, failed CPAP/MAD, Class II skeletal, candidate for MMA.
vignette.chief: Pre-surgical dental evaluation before planned maxillomandibular advancement.
vignette.clinical: Healthy teeth and periodontium, 6 mm overjet, impacted third molars.
vignette.radio: CBCT confirms reduced airway and presence of third molars.

questions.q: What is the most critical pre-surgical dental contribution before MMA for OSA?
options: Immediate extraction of all third molars only

Comprehensive periodontal and restorative clearance, assessment of occlusal stability, coordination of any necessary orthodontic decompensation, and planning for temporary MAD or interim appliance use during healing if needed
No dental input is required once the surgeon accepts the case
Fabrication of a permanent post-surgical MAD before osteotomy
questions.explanation: MMA success depends on healthy supporting structures and a stable post-surgical occlusion. Dental evaluation must clear active disease, address third molars if they interfere with osteotomy or fixation, coordinate orthodontic decompensation when indicated, and plan interim airway support during the healing phase.

questions.q: In a Class II patient undergoing MMA for OSA, what orthodontic consideration is frequently required?
options: No orthodontics is ever needed
Pre-surgical decompensation (often proclining lower incisors or coordinating arches) so that the surgical movements can maximize airway gain while finishing in a stable Class I occlusion
Only post-surgical alignment is permitted
Extraction of all premolars is mandatory
questions.explanation: Skeletal Class II patients often present with dental compensation. Controlled decompensation allows the surgeon to advance the mandible (and often maxilla) more fully, thereby maximizing pharyngeal airway enlargement while still achieving a functional Class I relationship.

questions.q: Red-team perioperative point: Why should residual OSA risk during the immediate post-MMA healing period be explicitly planned for?
options: MMA always cures OSA on the operating table

Soft-tissue edema, temporary malocclusion, and intermaxillary fixation or elastics can transiently worsen obstruction; bridging strategies (elevated head-of-bed, cautious narcotic use, temporary appliance or CPAP if compatible) are required
No airway risk exists after osteotomy
Only antibiotics are needed
questions.explanation: Even successful MMA carries a period of postoperative edema and altered occlusion that can increase obstruction risk. Multidisciplinary planning for airway protection, analgesia, and temporary support is a standard safety requirement.

title: High Smile Line + Thin Biotype — Missing Lateral Incisor Decision Tree
short: 24F • high smile line • thin scalloped biotype • congenitally missing #10

patient.medical_history: Healthy, non-smoker, no medications. Orthodontic treatment completed 18 months ago with space maintained at #10.
patient.chief_complaint: I hate the fake tooth on my retainer. I want a permanent, natural-looking solution before my wedding in 9 months.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: 1–3 mm throughout; no bleeding on probing. Thin periodontal phenotype (probe visible through gingiva).
clinical_findings.mobility: All teeth physiologic. #7 and #11 slightly upright after ortho.
clinical_findings.radiographs: CBCT: 6.2 mm mesio-distal space at crest, 5.8 mm at 3 mm apical; facial plate thickness 0.6 mm at crest; adequate vertical bone.

flags: High smile line (shows full clinical crowns + 2–3 mm gingiva)

vignette.demographics: 24-year-old healthy female, non-smoker. Completed orthodontics 18 months previously; space at #10 maintained with Essex retainer.
vignette.chief: "I hate the fake tooth on my retainer. I want something permanent and natural before my wedding in nine months."
vignette.clinical: High smile line revealing 2–3 mm of gingiva. Thin scalloped biotype. Mesio-distal space #10: 6.2 mm at crest. Adjacent laterals and canines healthy, no restorations. Gingival margins of #7 and #11 slightly asymmetric.
vignette.endo: All anterior teeth respond normally to cold and EPT. No sensitivity.
vignette.radio: CBCT confirms thin facial plate (0.6 mm), adequate ridge height, no periapical pathology. Root proximity of #9 and #11 acceptable for implant.

questions.q: Given the high smile line, thin biotype, and facial plate thickness of 0.6 mm, which treatment option carries the highest long-term risk of mid-facial recession and esthetic failure if performed as an immediate implant?
options: Immediate implant with simultaneous connective-tissue graft and custom healing abutment
Early implant placement (4–8 weeks) with guided bone regeneration and delayed provisionalization
Orthodontic space closure and canine substitution with enamel recontouring and bleaching
Three-unit zirconia fixed dental prosthesis using #9 and #11 as abutments
questions.explanation: Immediate placement into a site with facial plate <1 mm and thin biotype has the highest documented risk of mid-facial recession (ITI Esthetic Zone papers, Chen & Buser). Even with simultaneous soft-tissue grafting, the thin residual plate is prone to further resorption. Early placement with GBR allows soft-tissue healing and better control of the facial contour. Canine substitution and a 3-unit bridge avoid implant-related soft-tissue risks entirely but introduce other trade-offs (occlusion, preparation of virgin teeth).

questions.q: If the interdisciplinary team elects implant therapy, which soft-tissue management sequence is most evidence-based for maximizing the Pink Esthetic Score in a thin-biotype, high-smile-line patient?
options: Immediate implant + immediate provisional + no soft-tissue graft
Extraction → 6–8 weeks soft-tissue healing → implant with simultaneous subepithelial connective-tissue graft + custom healing abutment → delayed provisionalization after osseointegration
Immediate implant with only xenograft in the gap and no connective-tissue graft
Placement of a stock healing abutment and hope the phenotype thickens spontaneously
questions.explanation: In thin-biotype sites the evidence favors staged soft-tissue augmentation (CTG) at the time of implant placement or earlier, combined with a custom healing abutment or provisional that supports the papillae and facial contour. Immediate provisionalization on an immediate implant in a thin plate has higher recession rates. Spontaneous phenotype conversion does not reliably occur.

questions.q: Red-team consent point: Which statement must be documented before proceeding with any implant option in this patient?
options: That an implant will look better than any other option for the wedding photographs

That mid-facial recession risk remains elevated for life, that a connective-tissue graft may still be required later, and that alternative options (canine substitution or adhesive bridge) have been offered and declined
That no further soft-tissue procedures will ever be needed
That the thin facial plate will regenerate completely after implant placement
questions.explanation: Informed consent in the esthetic zone must explicitly address the lifelong recession risk in thin biotypes, the possible need for additional grafting, and documentation that less invasive alternatives were discussed. Over-promising stability or denying residual risk is a frequent source of later dissatisfaction and medico-legal exposure.

title: Severely Discolored Endodontically Treated Central — Internal Bleach vs Ceramic Decision
short: 32M • #8 RCT 6 yrs ago • dark gray discoloration • high esthetic demand

patient.medical_history: Healthy, no medications, non-smoker.
patient.chief_complaint: My front tooth is dark gray and looks dead in every photo. I want it to match the other teeth permanently.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: 1–3 mm, no BOP. Thick flat biotype.
clinical_findings.mobility: Physiologic. #8 has a small mesial composite and intact ferrule of 2.5 mm circumferentially.
clinical_findings.radiographs: PA and CBCT: previous RCT appears adequate, no apical lucency, no vertical root fracture, root walls of good thickness.

flags: Intrinsic gray discoloration of endodontically treated #8
Patient refuses 'any preparation of healthy enamel' if avoidable

vignette.demographics: 32-year-old healthy male, non-smoker, high esthetic demand.
vignette.chief: "My front tooth is dark gray and looks dead in every photo. I want it to match the other teeth permanently."
vignette.clinical: Tooth #8 exhibits uniform dark gray discoloration. Small mesial composite present. 2.5 mm of sound supragingival tooth structure circumferentially. Adjacent teeth unrestored, shade A1. High smile line.
vignette.endo: Previous RCT completed 6 years ago; tooth is asymptomatic, no sinus tract, normal probing.
vignette.radio: Adequate root canal fill, no apical pathology, no signs of resorption or fracture. Good remaining dentin thickness.

questions.q: According to current AAE and esthetic principles, what is the most conservative first-line approach that still offers a high probability of acceptable color correction for this tooth?
options: Immediate full-coverage lithium-disilicate crown
Walking bleach (internal sodium perborate or carbamide peroxide) after confirming coronal seal, followed by evaluation of residual discoloration before any ceramic decision
External in-office bleaching only
Direct composite veneer without addressing the internal discoloration
questions.explanation: AAE guidelines support internal (walking) bleach as the most conservative first step for intrinsically discolored endodontically treated teeth when the root canal is adequate and a coronal seal can be established. Many cases achieve sufficient lightening to allow a more conservative ceramic or even no ceramic. Jumping directly to a crown removes unnecessary tooth structure. External bleaching alone rarely corrects deep intrinsic gray discoloration. Composite without internal treatment often fails to mask the underlying color.

questions.q: If after two cycles of internal bleaching a residual gray hue remains that is unacceptable to the patient, which ceramic approach best balances esthetics, tooth conservation, and long-term ferrule preservation?
options: Conventional full-coverage zirconia crown with 1.5–2 mm axial reduction
Minimal-preparation or no-prep feldspathic or lithium-disilicate veneer after confirming adequate remaining enamel and bonding substrate
Porcelain-fused-to-metal crown for opacity
Extraction and immediate implant because the tooth is 'hopelessly discolored'
questions.explanation: With a confirmed 2.5 mm ferrule and intact enamel, a minimally invasive veneer can mask residual discoloration while preserving the maximum amount of tooth structure and the existing ferrule. Full-coverage crowns require more aggressive preparation and permanently weaken the tooth. PFM is optically inferior in the esthetic zone. Extraction is not indicated for a restorable, asymptomatic tooth.

questions.q: Red-team material and risk point: Why is immediate placement of an opaque zirconia crown without an internal bleaching attempt considered a lower-quality decision in this specific case?
options: Zirconia is never indicated for anterior teeth

It permanently removes enamel and dentin that could have been preserved, eliminates the chance of a more conservative solution, and commits the patient to a full-coverage restoration for life when a less invasive pathway still exists
Internal bleaching always fails, so the crown is inevitable
The ferrule is insufficient for a veneer
questions.explanation: The core principle of modern esthetic dentistry is progressive, tissue-preserving decision making. Bypassing internal bleaching and going straight to a full-coverage crown violates that principle when a more conservative option remains viable. It also eliminates future flexibility and increases the long-term biomechanical risk to the tooth.

title: Gummy Smile + Altered Passive Eruption — Sequencing Crown Lengthening with Veneers
short: 27F • excessive gingival display • short clinical crowns • thick biotype

patient.medical_history: Healthy, non-smoker.
patient.chief_complaint: I show too much gum when I smile and my front teeth look short and square. I want longer, more natural-looking teeth.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: 2–3 mm, no BOP. Thick flat biotype. Short clinical crowns with gingival margins incisal to the CEJ.
clinical_findings.radiographs: PA and CBCT: bone crest is 1–2 mm from CEJ on #6–11, confirming altered passive eruption Type 1B (bone crest close to CEJ).

flags: Patient desires veneers for shape and shade
guidelines: Coslet classification of altered passive eruption
Biologic width / supracrestal tissue attachment principles

vignette.demographics: 27-year-old healthy female with high esthetic demand.
vignette.chief: "I show too much gum when I smile and my front teeth look short and square. I want longer, more natural-looking teeth."
vignette.clinical: 4–5 mm gingival display on full smile. Clinical crowns of #7–10 appear short and square. Gingival margins are positioned incisal to the CEJ. Thick flat biotype. No inflammation.
vignette.radio: Bone crest located 1–2 mm from CEJ on the facial of #6–11, consistent with altered passive eruption Type 1B.

questions.q: According to the Coslet classification and current biologic-width principles, what is the correct surgical diagnosis and primary treatment for the gingival display in this patient?
options: Vertical maxillary excess requiring orthognathic surgery
Altered passive eruption Type 1B (gingiva and bone both coronal) requiring esthetic crown lengthening with osseous resection to establish proper CEJ-to-bone distance
Simple gingivectomy only, because the bone is already in the correct position
Botulinum toxin to the upper lip elevators as definitive therapy
questions.explanation: Coslet Type 1B is defined by gingival margins coronal to the CEJ and bone crest also close to the CEJ. Gingivectomy alone will relapse because the bone continues to support the soft tissue at an incorrect level. Proper treatment is flap elevation, osseous resection to create 2–3 mm of distance from CEJ to bone crest, and apical positioning of the flap. Vertical maxillary excess is a skeletal diagnosis that would show different facial proportions. Botox is adjunctive at best and does not address tooth proportion.

questions.q: What is the evidence-based sequence when both crown lengthening and ceramic veneers are planned?
options: Prepare and cement veneers first, then perform crown lengthening around the finished restorations
Perform esthetic crown lengthening, allow 3–6 months of soft-tissue maturation, then perform final veneer preparation and delivery using the new stable gingival levels
Prepare the teeth for veneers and perform crown lengthening at the same appointment
Crown lengthening is unnecessary if the veneers are made longer
questions.explanation: Soft tissue and bone need 3–6 months (sometimes longer) to stabilize after osseous crown lengthening. Preparing and cementing veneers before this maturation risks margin exposure, open gingival embrasures, or the need to remake the ceramics. The correct sequence is surgery → maturation → definitive prosthetic phase. Simultaneous preparation and surgery increases the chance of biologic-width violation and unpredictable gingival levels.

questions.q: Red-team planning error: A clinician performs only gingivectomy (no osseous resection) and delivers veneers 4 weeks later. What is the most likely long-term outcome?
options: Stable, ideal gingival levels and excellent Pink Esthetic Score
Gingival rebound toward the original position, progressive exposure of veneer margins, and possible need for revision surgery or remakes
Complete resolution of the gummy smile without further treatment
No consequences because the biotype is thick
questions.explanation: When bone is left at the CEJ, the soft tissue will re-establish its biologic width and migrate coronally again (rebound). Veneers delivered on unstable tissues frequently show margin exposure and black triangles within 6–24 months, requiring additional surgery and often new restorations. This is a classic avoidable sequencing error.

title: Multiple Diastemas + Bolton Discrepancy — Additive vs Subtractive Esthetic Strategy
short: 29F • generalized diastemas • small laterals • high smile line

patient.medical_history: Healthy, non-smoker.
patient.chief_complaint: I have spaces between all my front teeth and my side teeth look too small. I want a full, even smile without looking fake.

clinical_findings.radiographs: No pathology. Bolton analysis reveals significant anterior tooth-size discrepancy (laterals and canines undersized relative to centrals).

guidelines: Additive composite vs ceramic decision criteria

vignette.demographics: 29-year-old healthy female with high esthetic demand who declines brackets or long-term aligners.
vignette.chief: "I have spaces between all my front teeth and my side teeth look too small. I want a full, even smile without looking fake."
vignette.clinical: Diastemas present between #6–11. Lateral incisors and canines are small relative to the centrals (Bolton discrepancy). High smile line, healthy thick biotype, no restorations.
vignette.radio: No caries, no periapical disease, adequate root length and form.

questions.q: In the presence of a significant Bolton discrepancy and the patient’s refusal of orthodontic space consolidation, which overall strategy best respects both esthetic proportion and tooth conservation?
options: Aggressive preparation of the centrals to make them smaller so the laterals look relatively larger

Additive approach: diagnostic additive wax-up / mock-up, then predominantly additive composite or thin ceramic restorations that increase the size of the laterals and canines while closing diastemas, preserving the centrals as much as possible
Extraction of the small laterals and replacement with implants
Ignore the Bolton discrepancy and simply close the largest diastema with a single veneer
questions.explanation: When orthodontics is declined, the evidence-based and tissue-preserving pathway is additive. A diagnostic additive mock-up verifies that proportion can be achieved by enlarging the undersized teeth rather than reducing the correctly sized centrals. Subtractive preparation of already-proportional centrals is irreversible and biomechanically inferior. Extraction of healthy laterals is extreme and unjustified.

questions.q: Which material and design choice is most appropriate if the patient prioritizes minimal tooth preparation and possible future reversibility?
options: Conventional preparation lithium-disilicate veneers on all six anterior teeth
No-prep or minimal-prep additive feldspathic or lithium-disilicate veneers / composite resin restorations guided by the diagnostic mock-up
Full-coverage zirconia crowns on the laterals and canines
Direct composite without a diagnostic mock-up or proportion analysis
questions.explanation: Additive or no-prep ceramics (or high-quality composite) allow the clinician to achieve the planned proportions while removing little or no enamel. This preserves future options and reduces biomechanical risk. Conventional preparations and full-coverage crowns are unnecessarily destructive when an additive solution is feasible. Freehand composite without a mock-up frequently produces incorrect proportions and occlusal problems.

questions.q: Red-team proportion error: A clinician closes the diastemas by placing wide veneers only on the centrals, leaving the laterals untouched. What is the most likely esthetic result?
options: Ideal Golden Proportion and natural appearance
Centrals that appear oversized and square, violation of RED/Golden Proportion, and an unnatural smile that the patient may later reject
Perfect long-term stability because less porcelain is used
No impact on smile esthetics
questions.explanation: Esthetic dentistry is governed by proportion. Enlarging already-correct centrals while leaving small laterals creates a classic 'central dominance' deformity that looks artificial. The diagnostic mock-up exists precisely to prevent this error. Patients frequently notice the imbalance after delivery, leading to remakes or dissatisfaction.

title: Failed Porcelain Veneers with Recurrent Caries & Marginal Breakdown — Material & Prep Redesign
short: 41F • 8-year-old veneers #6–11 • recurrent caries • high smile line

patient.medical_history: Healthy, non-smoker, high caries risk history.
patient.chief_complaint: Several of my veneers have dark lines at the edges and two feel rough. I want them replaced so they look natural again.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: 1–3 mm, mild localized BOP at open margins.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Bitewings and PAs show radiolucencies under the margins of #7, #8, #10 consistent with recurrent caries. No apical pathology.

flags: Failing veneers with open margins and recurrent caries

vignette.demographics: 41-year-old female with previous porcelain veneers placed 8 years earlier.
vignette.chief: "Several of my veneers have dark lines at the edges and two feel rough. I want them replaced so they look natural again."
vignette.clinical: Veneers on #6–11. Open margins with catch and discoloration on #7, #8, #10. Mild gingival inflammation at defective margins. High smile line. Remaining enamel status after old preparations is uncertain.
vignette.radio: Radiographic evidence of recurrent caries under multiple margins. No pulpal or periapical involvement.

questions.q: Before any new ceramic is designed, what is the most critical clinical step after removal of the old veneers?
options: Immediately prepare for new full-coverage crowns because the teeth are 'compromised'
Complete caries excavation, evaluate remaining enamel quantity and quality, assess ferrule and bonding substrate, and only then decide between new veneers versus full coverage
Place temporary crowns and schedule the final impressions the next day
Apply silver diamine fluoride and rebond the old veneers
questions.explanation: After removal of failed veneers the substrate must be reassessed. Only after complete caries removal and evaluation of remaining enamel can the clinician decide whether a new veneer (still enamel-bonded) is feasible or whether the preparation must be converted to full coverage. Jumping to crowns without this evaluation is unnecessarily aggressive. Temporary restorations are needed, but the substrate decision precedes final preparation design.

questions.q: Assuming adequate enamel remains after caries removal, which combination of material and bonding protocol currently offers the best combination of optical quality and long-term retention for new anterior veneers?
options: Monolithic zirconia veneers bonded with self-adhesive resin cement
Feldspathic or lithium-disilicate veneers bonded with gold-standard etch-and-rinse adhesive technique, silane, and light-cured or dual-cured resin cement under strict isolation
Composite veneers without adhesive bonding
PMMA temporary material as the definitive restoration
questions.explanation: Current evidence still favors glass-ceramics (feldspathic or lithium disilicate) for the highest optical integration in the esthetic zone when enamel bonding is possible. The classic etch-and-rinse + silane + resin cement protocol under rubber dam or equivalent isolation remains the most predictable. Zirconia has inferior translucency and requires different surface treatment; self-adhesive cements alone are less reliable for veneers. Composite is more technique-sensitive long-term and optically inferior for multiple units.

questions.q: Red-team caries-risk point: What additional non-restorative measure is essential to protect the new veneers in this patient?
options: No additional measures are needed once the ceramics are bonded
Formal caries-risk reassessment, high-fluoride regimen, dietary counseling, and more frequent recall with professional monitoring of margins
Prescription of systemic antibiotics for 1 year
Immediate extraction of all remaining teeth and conversion to a full-arch prosthesis
questions.explanation: Patients who have already lost veneers to recurrent caries remain at elevated risk. Without active caries management the new restorations will likely fail by the same mechanism. CAMBRA-style risk reduction, fluoride, and closer surveillance are mandatory adjuncts to any new ceramic work.

title: Esthetic Zone Ridge Collapse After Extraction — Soft-Tissue & Provisional Strategy for Final Ceramic
short: 38F • #9 extracted 4 months ago • Seibert Class III defect • high smile line

patient.medical_history: Healthy, non-smoker. #9 extracted because of vertical root fracture; no grafting was performed at the time of extraction.
patient.chief_complaint: There is a big dent and black space where my front tooth was. I want a permanent tooth that looks real and fills the gum properly.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: Adjacent teeth healthy. Soft-tissue volume deficiency both horizontally and vertically at the #9 site.
clinical_findings.radiographs: CBCT: significant horizontal and vertical ridge deficiency (Seibert Class III). Adjacent roots intact, adequate inter-root distance for an implant if volume is reconstructed.

flags: Seibert Class III ridge defect in esthetic zone
No ridge preservation at time of extraction
guidelines: ITI soft- and hard-tissue reconstruction protocols
Pink Esthetic Score / White Esthetic Score
Provisionalization and ovate pontic or implant provisional design

vignette.demographics: 38-year-old healthy non-smoker. Tooth #9 lost to vertical root fracture 4 months earlier; no grafting performed.
vignette.chief: "There is a big dent and black space where my front tooth was. I want a permanent tooth that looks real and fills the gum properly."
vignette.clinical: Marked horizontal and vertical soft- and hard-tissue deficiency at #9. High smile line. Adjacent teeth #8 and #10 healthy and unrestored. Black triangle and ridge collapse visible on smile.
vignette.radio: CBCT confirms Seibert Class III defect. Bone volume insufficient for ideal implant placement without reconstruction.

questions.q: What is the most predictable overall strategy for achieving both ideal implant position and high Pink Esthetic Score in this Seibert Class III esthetic-zone defect?
options: Immediate implant placement with only a cover screw and hope soft tissue fills in

Staged approach: horizontal and vertical ridge reconstruction (guided bone regeneration ± soft-tissue grafting) → maturation → implant placement in the reconstructed volume → further soft-tissue refinement if needed → provisionalization that sculpts the emergence profile → final ceramic
Maryland bridge only, accepting the ridge defect
Three-unit conventional bridge with ovate pontic and no attempt at ridge reconstruction
questions.explanation: Seibert Class III defects in the esthetic zone almost never yield ideal implant position or soft-tissue volume with a single-stage immediate approach. The evidence-based pathway is staged hard- and soft-tissue reconstruction, followed by implant placement into the rebuilt ridge, then provisionalization that develops the emergence profile. Accepting the defect with a pontic or Maryland bridge is possible but rarely satisfies a high smile-line patient who wants 'real' pink-and-white esthetics.

questions.q: During the provisional phase after implant uncovering, what is the primary purpose of a properly contoured screw-retained provisional or custom healing abutment?
options: Only to keep the patient from being edentulous
To sculpt and maintain the soft-tissue architecture (facial contour and papillae) so that the final ceramic can emerge from healthy, stable tissue with an optimal Pink Esthetic Score
To load the implant immediately in all cases
To avoid the need for any soft-tissue grafting
questions.explanation: The provisional is a critical soft-tissue management tool. Its subgingival contour supports the facial gingiva and papillae, guiding the tissue into the desired architecture before the final impression. Without this step the final crown often emerges from collapsed or flat tissue, producing a poor Pink Esthetic Score even if the implant is perfectly placed.

questions.q: Red-team sequencing error: A clinician places an implant into the unrestored Class III defect, immediately loads a stock temporary, and delivers the final crown 3 months later. What is the most likely esthetic outcome?
options: Ideal Pink and White Esthetic Scores

Facial recession or flat gingival architecture, possible gray show-through, black triangles, and a final result that appears 'long' or unnatural — frequently requiring later soft-tissue grafting and remake of the crown
Complete spontaneous regeneration of the lost ridge
No soft-tissue consequences because the implant is osseointegrated
questions.explanation: Placing an implant into an unreconstructed Class III defect and skipping provisional soft-tissue sculpting almost predictably produces compromised pink esthetics. Patients with high smile lines notice the flat or recessed gingiva, gray hue, and open embrasures. Secondary grafting and crown remakes then become necessary — an avoidable, more complex, and more expensive pathway.

title: Deploying Soldier with Deep Caries & Symptomatic Pulpitis — DRC Assignment
short: 24M • Active Duty • Imminent deployment in 10 days • Deep caries #19

patient.medical_history: Healthy, no meds, NKDA. Active-duty Army, scheduled for 9-month deployment to austere environment in 10 days.
patient.chief_complaint: Sharp pain to cold on lower left molar for 5 days; keeps me awake at night.

clinical_findings.radiographs: PA #19: deep occlusal caries approaching pulp, early PDL widening at apex, no frank radiolucency.

guidelines: Tactical Combat Casualty Care dental considerations

vignette.demographics: 24 y/o healthy active-duty male, 10 days from deployment to austere location with limited dental assets.
vignette.chief: Sharp, lingering cold pain #19 for 5 days, nocturnal symptoms.
vignette.clinical: Deep occlusal caries #19, positive lingering cold response, negative percussion, no swelling.
vignette.endo: Cold: lingering pain >10 s; EPT responsive; percussion negative.
vignette.radio: Deep caries near pulp; early apical PDL widening; no established radiolucency.

questions.q: According to current DoD Dental Readiness Classification criteria, what is the correct DRC assignment for this Soldier if definitive endodontic treatment cannot be completed before deployment?
options: DRC 1 — fully ready; symptoms are manageable with analgesics
DRC 2 — treatment needed but not expected to cause problems within 12 months
DRC 3 — urgent/emergency condition expected to result in dental emergency within 12 months if not treated
DRC 4 — classification unknown pending further evaluation
questions.explanation: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis with nocturnal pain is classified as DRC 3. DoD criteria designate conditions expected to cause a dental emergency (pain, infection) within the deployment window as non-deployable until treated or stabilized. Analgesics alone do not convert DRC 3 to DRC 2. DRC 1 requires no treatment needs; DRC 4 is reserved for unexamined personnel.

questions.q: If definitive RCT cannot be completed before wheels-up, what is the most appropriate operational temporization strategy?
options: Extraction of #19 in the field dental clinic immediately
Pulpotomy or pulpectomy with intracanal medicament + provisional restoration, followed by clear documentation and follow-up plan for the receiving theater dental asset
Prescribe antibiotics and analgesics only and clear for deployment as DRC 2
Place a direct pulp cap and permanent restoration
questions.explanation: When definitive RCT cannot be finished, a pulpotomy/pulpectomy with Ca(OH)₂ or similar medicament plus a secure provisional is the evidence-based temporization that reduces emergency risk. Extraction is irreversible and not required if the tooth is restorable. Antibiotics alone are inappropriate for irreversible pulpitis without infection. Direct pulp cap is contraindicated once irreversible pulpitis is established.

questions.q: Red-team readiness decision: Which statement best reflects current DoD policy regarding deployment of a Soldier with an incompletely treated endodontic emergency?
options: Any endodontic treatment started automatically returns the Soldier to DRC 1
Command may waive DRC 3 for mission-essential personnel after risk acknowledgment, but the dental officer must still document residual risk and recommended follow-up
No Soldier with any open endodontic access may deploy under any circumstances
Once antibiotics are prescribed the classification automatically becomes DRC 2
questions.explanation: Commanders retain final deployment authority and may accept residual risk for mission-essential personnel; however, the dental officer is obligated to assign the correct DRC, document residual risk, and provide a clear follow-up plan. Automatic reclassification to DRC 1 or 2 after incomplete treatment or antibiotics is incorrect and creates false readiness reporting.

title: Battlefield Dental Trauma — Avulsed Tooth in Austere Environment
short: 28M • Combat arms • Avulsion #8 • 45 min dry time • Limited field assets

patient.medical_history: Healthy, tetanus current, no allergies. Forward operating base with Role 1/2 dental capability only.
patient.chief_complaint: Tooth knocked out during blast event 45 minutes ago; tooth recovered dry from dirt.

clinical_findings.mobility: Socket empty, minimal alveolar fracture on clinical exam.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Field PA if available: empty socket #8, no root fragments visible.

guidelines: TCCC / dental trauma in austere settings

vignette.demographics: 28 y/o combat arms male, closed apex #8 avulsed 45 min earlier, dry storage in contaminated environment.
vignette.chief: Tooth out of mouth, recovered from dirt.
vignette.clinical: Empty socket, mild soft-tissue laceration, no obvious alveolar fracture, tooth has closed apex, some debris.
vignette.radio: Field radiograph if obtainable confirms empty socket.

questions.q: According to IADT 2020 adapted for austere/military settings, what is the most appropriate immediate management of the avulsed #8 with 45 min dry time?
options: Discard the tooth; success rates after >30–60 min dry time are too low to justify replantation risk
Rinse debris gently, replant as soon as possible, stabilize with flexible splint, and plan for timely endodontic therapy
Store in milk or saline and evacuate to Role 3 before any attempt at replantation
Perform immediate root-end resection and intentional replantation
questions.explanation: Even with extended dry time, IADT still recommends attempting replantation for permanent teeth when feasible. Dry time >60 min carries high ankylosis risk, but 45 min remains within a window where replantation is preferred over immediate discard. Gentle rinsing (no scrubbing), rapid replantation, flexible splinting, and subsequent endodontic therapy constitute the standard sequence. Evacuation without attempting replantation loses the critical extra-oral time window.

questions.q: In a Role 1/2 setting with limited endodontic capability, what is the preferred timing and method for pulp management after replantation of a closed-apex tooth with prolonged dry time?
options: Immediate root canal treatment before replantation
Initiate endodontic therapy within 7–14 days using calcium hydroxide or equivalent medicament; avoid immediate RCT if possible
Wait for spontaneous pulp revascularization; closed-apex teeth frequently recover vitality
Extract after 2 weeks regardless of clinical status
questions.explanation: For closed-apex teeth with extended extra-oral dry time, pulp necrosis is expected. IADT recommends initiating RCT within 7–14 days post-replantation (after initial soft-tissue healing) with an intracanal medicament. Immediate extra-oral RCT is no longer preferred. Revascularization is not realistic in mature teeth. Planned extraction is not the default.

questions.q: Red-team operational point: After successful field replantation and temporary stabilization, what is the correct Dental Readiness Classification and disposition recommendation?
options: DRC 1 — Soldier is fully ready for unrestricted duty
DRC 2 — monitor only; no further treatment expected
DRC 3 — requires definitive endodontic and restorative care; non-deployable or limited duty until stabilized and followed by theater dental assets
Automatic medical evacuation to CONUS regardless of clinical stability
questions.explanation: A recently replanted tooth with pending endodontic therapy remains at high risk for infection, resorption, or loss and is therefore DRC 3 until definitive treatment and a period of stability are achieved. Automatic CONUS evacuation is not mandated if theater assets can manage the case; disposition is driven by residual risk and mission requirements.

title: Asymptomatic but High-Risk Third Molars — Pre-Deployment Decision
short: 22M • Marine • Partially erupted #17 & #32 • No symptoms • Deployment in 6 weeks

patient.medical_history: Healthy. Scheduled for shipboard deployment with limited dental surgical capability.
patient.chief_complaint: None; routine pre-deployment dental exam.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: 5–6 mm distal to #17 and #32 with food impaction; soft-tissue operculum present.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Pano: mesioangular partially erupted #17 and #32, roots near but not compressing IAN canal; no cystic change.

vignette.demographics: 22 y/o healthy Marine, 6 weeks from shipboard deployment.
vignette.chief: Asymptomatic; routine screening.
vignette.clinical: Partially erupted #17/#32 with opercula and 5–6 mm distal probing; history of occasional food trapping.
vignette.radio: Mesioangular impactions, roots clear of IAN, no pathology.

questions.q: In the context of an imminent shipboard deployment with limited oral-surgery capability, what is the most appropriate readiness recommendation for these partially erupted third molars?
options: Leave in place; asymptomatic third molars never require prophylactic removal
Extract both #17 and #32 before deployment if time and healing window allow, converting the Soldier/Marine to DRC 1
Classify as DRC 2 and deploy with chlorhexidine rinse only
Extract only if the patient develops acute pericoronitis in theater
questions.explanation: Military policy and AAOMS guidance support prophylactic removal of partially erupted third molars with soft-tissue coverage and probing depths that predispose to pericoronitis when the service member is deploying to an environment with limited surgical assets. A 6-week window usually permits extraction and adequate soft-tissue healing. Deploying known high-risk third molars as DRC 2 increases the probability of a preventable dental emergency at sea.

questions.q: If extraction is chosen, what is the minimum recommended healing interval before unrestricted operational duty in most military dental readiness guidance?
options: 24 hours
3–5 days with primary closure and no complications
Approximately 7–14 days of soft-tissue healing before high-risk physical activity or deployment
6 months of bony remodeling
questions.explanation: Most service-branch guidance and practical experience require roughly 7–14 days of soft-tissue healing after uncomplicated third-molar removal before return to full operational or high-impact activity. Twenty-four hours is insufficient; 6 months of bony healing is not required for readiness classification.

questions.q: Red-team risk communication: What is the most accurate counseling point when recommending pre-deployment third-molar removal?
options: There is zero risk of nerve injury or dry socket
The risk of a preventable pericoronitis or infection emergency in an austere/shipboard environment outweighs the low but real surgical risks of extraction in a controlled CONUS setting
Extraction is required by regulation for every third molar regardless of position
Leaving the teeth and treating acute pericoronitis in theater is always safer
questions.explanation: Informed consent must balance the documented risk of pericoronitis/infection in partially erupted third molars against the low incidence of nerve injury and alveolar osteitis when surgery is performed under controlled conditions. Blanket statements of zero risk or mandatory extraction of every third molar are inaccurate. Theater treatment of acute pericoronitis is possible but carries higher operational cost and morbidity.

title: Acute Odontogenic Infection in Forward Environment — Airway & Evacuation Decision
short: 31M • Infantry • Rapidly progressive submandibular swelling • Role 1 aid station

patient.medical_history: Healthy. Forward operating base, Role 1 medical capability only; nearest Role 2/3 is 4-hour ground evacuation.
patient.chief_complaint: Lower right toothache for 4 days; floor of mouth and neck swelling for 12 hours; difficulty swallowing saliva.

clinical_findings.radiographs: Field PA: large periapical radiolucency #30.

vignette.demographics: 31 y/o infantry male at Role 1, 4-hour evacuation to higher care.
vignette.chief: Progressive submandibular and floor-of-mouth swelling with dysphagia.
vignette.clinical: Firm floor-of-mouth elevation, tongue elevation, mild trismus, febrile, #30 non-restorable.
vignette.radio: Large apical radiolucency #30.

questions.q: In a Role 1 setting, what is the single most important immediate action?
options: Start oral antibiotics and observe for 24 hours
Secure or prepare for airway (including early evacuation decision) because floor-of-mouth elevation and dysphagia signal impending airway compromise
Perform immediate extraction of #30 under local anesthesia only
Apply warm compresses and reassess in the morning
questions.explanation: Floor-of-mouth elevation with dysphagia is a red-flag for impending airway loss (Ludwig angina spectrum). In austere settings the priority is airway assessment/preparation and rapid evacuation decision, not observation or immediate surgical source control under suboptimal conditions. Source control follows once airway is secure and appropriate level of care is reached.

questions.q: Which antibiotic choice is most appropriate as an adjunct while arranging evacuation?
options: Oral penicillin VK alone

IV or IM broad-spectrum coverage that includes aerobic and anaerobic oral flora (e.g., ampicillin-sulbactam or equivalent available field agent) plus consideration of additional anaerobic coverage if progressing
Topical antibiotics only
No antibiotics until culture results are obtained
questions.explanation: Rapidly progressive odontogenic deep-space infection requires prompt systemic antibiotics covering oral aerobes and anaerobes. Field formularies vary, but the principle is early, broad coverage while evacuating. Oral penicillin alone is insufficient for deep-space disease; cultures should not delay therapy.

questions.q: Red-team evacuation criterion: Which finding most strongly mandates priority evacuation rather than continued observation at Role 1?
options: Mild toothache without swelling
Floor-of-mouth firmness, tongue elevation, or any sign of airway involvement
Low-grade fever alone
Patient preference to remain with unit
questions.explanation: Any clinical sign of floor-of-mouth or deep-neck involvement is an absolute indication for priority evacuation to a facility capable of definitive airway management and surgical drainage. Mild toothache or isolated low-grade fever does not meet the same threshold.

title: Chronic Periodontitis in a Senior NCO — Deployability vs Progressive Attachment Loss
short: 42M • Senior NCO • Generalized Stage III Grade B • Deployment in 30 days

patient.medical_history: Former smoker (quit 3 yrs), well-controlled HTN. Mission-essential billet.
patient.chief_complaint: Bleeding gums and bad taste; wants to know if he can deploy.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: 5–7 mm generalized, localized 8 mm; BOP 60%; horizontal bone loss 40–50%.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Horizontal bone loss, no vertical defects >3 mm, no acute abscess.

vignette.demographics: 42 y/o senior NCO, former smoker, controlled HTN, mission-essential, 30 days to deployment.
vignette.chief: Chronic bleeding and halitosis; deployability question.
vignette.clinical: Generalized 5–7 mm pockets, high BOP, Class I mobility several teeth, no suppuration or acute abscess.
vignette.radio: Moderate horizontal bone loss, no advanced vertical defects.

questions.q: Under current DoD Dental Readiness criteria, how should this service member most likely be classified if only non-surgical scaling and root planing can be completed before deployment?
options: DRC 1 after a single SRP visit
DRC 2 if acute infection is absent and a maintenance plan is documented
Automatic DRC 3 because any Stage III disease is non-deployable
DRC 4 until full periodontal charting is repeated in theater
questions.explanation: Chronic periodontitis without acute infection, abscess, or uncontrolled pain is generally managed as DRC 2 provided initial therapy is started and a clear maintenance/follow-up plan exists. Stage III alone does not automatically equal DRC 3; acute conditions drive DRC 3. A single SRP does not restore DRC 1.

questions.q: What is the highest-yield pre-deployment periodontal intervention within a 30-day window?
options: Full-mouth extraction of all Grade B teeth
Thorough non-surgical SRP, oral-hygiene reinforcement, short-term chlorhexidine, and documentation of residual risk + theater maintenance plan
Immediate osseous surgery on all residual pockets
Systemic antibiotics alone without mechanical debridement
questions.explanation: Within a short window the evidence-based approach is high-quality non-surgical therapy, hygiene optimization, and risk documentation. Surgical osseous recontouring is not feasible or indicated as a rushed pre-deployment procedure. Antibiotics without debridement are ineffective long-term.

questions.q: Red-team command counseling point: What residual risk must be explicitly communicated?
options: Zero risk of periodontal emergency once SRP is performed
Residual risk of acute periodontal abscess or accelerated attachment loss under operational stress, tobacco relapse, or poor hygiene; therefore theater dental follow-up is required
Periodontal disease has no impact on operational readiness
Only bleeding on probing matters; pocket depth is irrelevant
questions.explanation: Even after SRP, Stage III patients retain elevated risk of acute exacerbation, especially under sleep deprivation, dietary change, or tobacco relapse common in deployment. Accurate risk communication and a theater maintenance plan are mandatory for ethical readiness reporting.

title: Field-Expedient Temporary Restoration & Fracture Management
short: 26F • Aircrew • Fractured #9 cusp with exposed dentin • 48 h to next dental asset

patient.medical_history: Healthy aircrew member; currently on temporary duty with only basic medical kit available.
patient.chief_complaint: Broke a piece of front tooth on a ration; sensitive to air and cold.

clinical_findings.radiographs: None available in current location.

flags: No rotary instruments or definitive materials

vignette.demographics: 26 y/o healthy aircrew, remote location, 48 h until next dental capability.
vignette.chief: Fractured mesial-incisal of #9 with dentin exposure and air sensitivity.
vignette.clinical: Uncomplicated crown fracture, no pulp exposure, positive vitality, no mobility or periodontal injury.
vignette.radio: Unavailable.

questions.q: In a truly austere setting without rotary instruments or composite, what is the most appropriate immediate field management?
options: Extract the tooth to eliminate sensitivity

Cover exposed dentin with a glass-ionomer or resin-modified glass-ionomer temporary material (or zinc-oxide eugenol if that is all that is available), smooth sharp edges, and arrange definitive care within 48–72 h
Leave the tooth untreated; dentin sensitivity is self-limiting
Perform a field pulpotomy prophylactically
questions.explanation: Uncomplicated crown fracture with dentin exposure is managed by protecting the dentin, eliminating sharp edges, and arranging timely definitive restoration. Glass-ionomer or RMGI is preferred when available; ZOE is an acceptable field expedient. Extraction or prophylactic pulpotomy is overtreatment. Leaving exposed dentin risks pulpitis and continued operational distraction.

questions.q: From a Dental Readiness standpoint, how should this service member be classified until definitive restoration is completed?
options: DRC 1 — no further treatment needed
DRC 2 — condition unlikely to cause emergency within the short window if temporized
DRC 3 — any fractured tooth is automatically non-deployable
DRC 4 — classification impossible without radiographs
questions.explanation: Once dentin is protected and symptoms are controlled, an uncomplicated crown fracture is appropriately managed as DRC 2 for short intervals. It does not meet DRC 3 criteria (expected emergency within 12 months) if temporized. Radiographs are ideal but not required for this classification decision.

questions.q: Red-team aircrew consideration: Why is prompt management of even a “simple” anterior fracture operationally important?
options: It has no operational impact
Air sensitivity and sharp edges can distract from flight duties, create speech or seal problems with oxygen masks, and risk pulpitis that becomes an in-flight emergency
Only posterior teeth matter for aircrew
Cosmetic appearance is the sole concern
questions.explanation: In aircrew, anterior tooth sensitivity or sharp edges can interfere with oxygen-mask seal, speech clarity, and concentration. Progression to irreversible pulpitis creates a potential in-flight medical event. Therefore even “simple” fractures receive priority temporization and early definitive care.

title: Incidental CBCT Finding — Large Unilocular Radiolucency in the Posterior Mandible
short: 42F • Asymptomatic • CBCT ordered for implant planning #19 site

patient.medical_history: Healthy, non-smoker, no medications.
patient.chief_complaint: Referred for implant evaluation at edentulous #19 site. No pain or swelling.

clinical_findings.radiographs: CBCT reveals a well-defined unilocular radiolucency 18 × 14 mm in the right posterior mandible, apical to and slightly distal to the mental foramen, with mild expansion and thinning of the buccal cortex. No root resorption of adjacent teeth. Inferior alveolar canal displaced inferiorly.

guidelines: WHO Classification of Odontogenic Cysts & Tumors

vignette.demographics: 42-year-old healthy female, non-smoker.
vignette.chief: Asymptomatic; CBCT obtained solely for implant planning at #19.
vignette.clinical: No expansion palpable. Soft tissues normal. Vitality testing of #18, #20, #21 within normal limits.
vignette.endo: All adjacent teeth respond normally to cold and EPT.
vignette.radio: Well-corticated unilocular radiolucency with inferior displacement of the IAC. Mild buccal expansion. No internal calcifications.

questions.q: According to current AAOMR principles and differential diagnosis hierarchy for a well-defined unilocular radiolucency in this location, which entity must be placed highest on the differential until proven otherwise?
options: Simple (traumatic) bone cyst
Odontogenic keratocyst (OKC) or unicystic ameloblastoma
Residual cyst from prior extraction
Stafne (static) bone defect
questions.explanation: In an adult with a well-defined unilocular radiolucency in the posterior mandible showing cortical expansion and IAC displacement, odontogenic keratocyst and unicystic ameloblastoma must head the differential because of their growth potential and recurrence risk. Simple bone cyst typically shows scalloping and no expansion; residual cyst requires a history of extraction in the exact site; Stafne defect is corticated, below the IAC, and contains salivary tissue — none of which fully match the imaging features here. AAOMR and pathology consensus require tissue diagnosis for any lesion with expansion or critical structure involvement.

questions.q: What is the most appropriate next imaging or diagnostic step before any surgical intervention?
options: No further imaging; proceed directly to enucleation
Contrast-enhanced MRI to assess soft-tissue involvement and solid vs cystic content
Repeat panoramic radiograph only
Immediate implant placement with simultaneous curettage
questions.explanation: CBCT is excellent for bony detail but limited for soft-tissue characterization. Contrast-enhanced MRI helps distinguish purely cystic from solid or mixed lesions (critical for ameloblastoma vs OKC vs other) and evaluates any soft-tissue extension. Proceeding to surgery without better characterization risks incomplete treatment of an aggressive entity. Panoramic adds little once CBCT is available; implant placement into an undiagnosed lesion is contraindicated.

questions.q: Red-team / risk-management: The referring dentist asks whether the implant can still be placed at #19 after the lesion is addressed. What is the most accurate counseling point?
options: Implant can be placed the same day as enucleation in all cases
Final implant timing and site suitability depend entirely on the histopathologic diagnosis, size of residual defect, and need for grafting or resection margins
Any radiolucency can be ignored if the patient is asymptomatic
CBCT dose is so low that serial observation without diagnosis is preferred indefinitely
questions.explanation: Histopathology dictates everything: a simple bone cyst may allow immediate or early implant placement after curettage; an OKC requires complete enucleation ± peripheral ostectomy and longer follow-up; ameloblastoma may require resection with margins. Residual defect size and cortical integrity further influence grafting needs and timing. Asymptomatic status does not eliminate the need for diagnosis. Indefinite observation of an expanding lesion near the IAC is not defensible.

title: CBCT for Impacted Canine — Root Resorption Risk Assessment
short: 14F • Impacted maxillary canine • Root resorption concern on #8

patient.medical_history: Healthy, orthodontic treatment planning.
patient.chief_complaint: Orthodontist requests CBCT to evaluate impacted #11 and possible resorption of #8 and #9.

clinical_findings.radiographs: CBCT shows palatally impacted #11 with crown contacting the apical third of the root of #8. Mild external root resorption of #8 (approximately 1.5–2 mm loss of apical root structure). Follicle of #11 measures 4 mm.

guidelines: AAOMR / AAO joint statement on CBCT

vignette.demographics: 14-year-old healthy female in orthodontic planning.
vignette.chief: Impacted maxillary left canine; concern for adjacent root resorption.
vignette.clinical: Palatal bulge palpable. #11 not visible. #8 and #9 respond normally to vitality testing.
vignette.endo: Vitality testing normal for adjacent teeth.
vignette.radio: CBCT: palatal impaction of #11, crown against apical third of #8 root with mild external resorption. Follicle 4 mm. Lateral incisor root otherwise intact.

questions.q: According to AAOMR and AAO guidance, when is CBCT most clearly indicated over conventional radiographs for an impacted maxillary canine?
options: In every orthodontic case involving an impacted canine
When conventional imaging suggests possible root resorption, close proximity to critical structures, or when 3-D localization will materially change the treatment plan
Only after surgical exposure has already been performed
Never; panoramic and occlusal films are always sufficient
questions.explanation: The AAOMR/AAO joint position and SEDENTEXCT emphasize that CBCT should be used when the additional 3-D information is expected to change diagnosis or treatment. Suspected root resorption, precise localization relative to the IAN or nasal floor, or complex surgical planning are classic indications. Routine use in every impacted canine is not supported; post-exposure imaging is too late for planning; conventional films remain first-line when they answer the clinical question.

questions.q: Given the CBCT finding of mild apical external resorption on #8 caused by the impacted canine, what is the most evidence-based statement regarding prognosis and management?
options: Any degree of resorption mandates immediate extraction of the lateral incisor
Mild resorption often stabilizes once the canine is moved away; the lateral should be monitored and can frequently be retained long-term
Resorption will inevitably progress to pulp necrosis regardless of orthodontic movement
CBCT overestimates resorption; therefore no clinical action is required
questions.explanation: Longitudinal studies (Ericson & Kurol and subsequent CBCT research) show that mild resorption frequently arrests once the pressure from the canine is removed. Extraction of the lateral is reserved for severe resorption that compromises restorability or when the tooth becomes non-vital and unrestorable. Pulp necrosis is not inevitable. CBCT is more accurate than 2-D for detecting and quantifying resorption; findings should not be dismissed.

questions.q: Radiation-protection / red-team point: The parent asks why a CBCT is needed when a panoramic was already taken. What is the most accurate response consistent with ALARA and AAOMR principles?
options: CBCT has essentially zero risk, so it can be used liberally

The decision balances the diagnostic benefit of detecting/characterizing resorption and 3-D position against the higher effective dose of CBCT; in this case the potential change in treatment plan justifies the exposure
Panoramic films never miss root resorption
CBCT is required by insurance for all impacted canines
questions.explanation: ALARA and AAOMR selection criteria require justification: the benefit of the additional information must outweigh the increased dose. Here, confirmation and quantification of resorption plus precise surgical-orthodontic planning provide that justification. CBCT is not zero-risk, panoramic films can miss early resorption, and insurance coverage is irrelevant to the clinical justification process.

title: Pre-Implant CBCT — Severe Buccal Plate Deficiency and Sinus Anatomy
short: 58M • Edentulous #3–#5 sites • Thin residual ridge + sinus proximity

patient.medical_history: Controlled hypertension, former smoker (quit 8 years).
patient.chief_complaint: Wants fixed implant reconstruction of the upper right posterior quadrant.

clinical_findings.radiographs: CBCT shows residual ridge height 4–5 mm to sinus floor, buccal plate thickness <0.5 mm or absent in places, and a septated sinus with a low-lying septum at the #4 site. Schneiderian membrane thickness 3 mm.

vignette.demographics: 58-year-old male, controlled HTN, former smoker.
vignette.chief: Fixed implant restoration of edentulous #3–#5.
vignette.clinical: Seibert Class III ridge deficiency clinically. High smile line not an issue in posterior.
vignette.radio: CBCT: 4–5 mm residual height, near-absent buccal plate, septated sinus, membrane 3 mm.

questions.q: What is the primary diagnostic value of CBCT over panoramic radiography in this pre-implant scenario?
options: CBCT is required only to measure length; width is irrelevant
Accurate 3-D quantification of residual bone height and width, buccal plate integrity, sinus septa, and membrane status — all of which directly determine grafting approach and implant feasibility
Panoramic films are equally accurate for sinus anatomy
CBCT is used mainly for marketing purposes
questions.explanation: Panoramic radiography provides only 2-D height approximation and cannot assess bucco-lingual width, plate thickness, or precise septal anatomy. CBCT supplies the metric data required for deciding between lateral-window sinus elevation, transcrestal approach, staged grafting, or alternative prosthetic plans. Membrane thickness and septa influence surgical difficulty and risk of perforation.

questions.q: Given residual height of 4–5 mm and near-absent buccal plate, which statement best reflects current evidence-based surgical planning?
options: Standard-length implants can be placed without any grafting
Lateral-window sinus elevation with simultaneous or staged grafting, plus horizontal augmentation consideration, is typically required for predictable fixed reconstruction
Zygomatic implants are first-line in every posterior maxillary case
Removable partial denture is the only acceptable option
questions.explanation: With <5–6 mm residual height, most protocols favor lateral-window sinus grafting (simultaneous if primary stability can be achieved, otherwise staged). The deficient buccal plate further necessitates horizontal augmentation or careful implant positioning. Short implants may be considered in selected cases but still often require grafting for width. Zygomatic implants are reserved for more extreme atrophy. RPDs remain an alternative but are not the only option when the patient desires fixed reconstruction.

questions.q: Red-team point: The patient asks whether a lower-dose ‘limited FOV’ scan would have been sufficient. What is the most accurate reply?
options: Any FOV is acceptable as long as the teeth are visible

A limited FOV centered on the implant sites can be appropriate and is preferred when it captures the necessary anatomic information (ridge, sinus floor, septa) while adhering to ALARA; larger FOVs increase dose without added benefit if the clinical question is site-specific
Full maxillofacial FOV is always mandatory for implant planning
Dose is irrelevant once the decision for CBCT has been made
questions.explanation: AAOMR and SEDENTEXCT emphasize the smallest FOV that answers the clinical question. For posterior maxillary implant planning, a limited FOV that includes the residual ridge and relevant sinus anatomy is usually sufficient and lower dose. Larger FOVs are justified only when additional structures (TMJ, full arch, pathology) must be evaluated. Dose optimization remains relevant after the decision to image has been made.

title: Suspected Vertical Root Fracture — Imaging Selection and Interpretation Limits
short: 51F • Persistent sinus tract after RCT #14 • Suspect VRF

patient.medical_history: Healthy.
patient.chief_complaint: Chronic draining sinus tract on the buccal of #14 two years after root canal therapy and crown placement.

clinical_findings.probing_depths: Narrow deep probing defect to 9 mm on the mid-buccal of #14; other sites ≤3 mm.
clinical_findings.radiographs: Periapical shows J-shaped radiolucency. CBCT shows a discrete buccal cortical discontinuity and vertical bone loss pattern suggestive of fracture, but the fracture line itself is not definitively visualized within the root.

guidelines: AAE Colleagues for Excellence – Vertical Root Fracture

vignette.demographics: 51-year-old healthy female.
vignette.chief: Persistent buccal sinus tract #14 after RCT and crown.
vignette.clinical: Isolated narrow deep probing defect mid-buccal. Crown margins appear clinically acceptable.
vignette.endo: Previous RCT; tooth is crowned and not retested for vitality.
vignette.radio: PA: classic J-shaped lucency. CBCT: buccal plate dehiscence and vertical bone loss; fracture line not clearly seen inside the root.

questions.q: What is the most accurate statement regarding CBCT for detection of vertical root fracture in an endodontically treated, restored tooth?
options: CBCT has near-100 % sensitivity and specificity for VRF in all cases

CBCT can support the diagnosis when classic patterns (J-shaped lesion, isolated vertical bone loss, cortical discontinuity) are present, but metal and gutta-percha artifacts frequently obscure the actual fracture line; clinical correlation and sometimes surgical exploration remain necessary
CBCT is never indicated for suspected VRF
A negative CBCT definitively rules out VRF
questions.explanation: Literature consistently shows that beam-hardening and streak artifacts from gutta-percha, posts, and crowns reduce CBCT sensitivity for the fracture line itself. Secondary signs (bone loss pattern, cortical breach) increase suspicion but are not pathognomonic. A negative scan does not exclude VRF; a positive scan still requires clinical confirmation. Surgical exploration or extraction with visual inspection remains the gold standard in many cases.

questions.q: Given the clinical narrow probing defect + J-shaped lesion + CBCT cortical discontinuity, what is the most appropriate next management step?
options: Nonsurgical retreatment only
Discussion of extraction and replacement options, with possible exploratory surgery if the patient desires an attempt at retention and the restorative prognosis is otherwise favorable
Antibiotic therapy alone for 6 months
Immediate implant placement without further evaluation
questions.explanation: The combination of findings is highly suggestive of VRF. Nonsurgical retreatment alone will not resolve a fracture. Antibiotics do not address the structural problem. Extraction is often definitive; exploratory surgery can confirm the fracture and allow assessment of whether the tooth is restorable after possible root amputation or other procedures in carefully selected cases. Implant planning occurs after the diagnosis is settled.

questions.q: Red-team imaging point: The patient asks why another CBCT was needed after the periapical film already showed a problem. Best response?
options: Periapical films are obsolete

CBCT provides 3-D information about the pattern and extent of bone loss and cortical integrity that helps differentiate VRF from pure endodontic failure or periodontal disease and aids surgical planning, while still acknowledging its limitations for visualizing the fracture line itself
CBCT was ordered only because the insurance required it
One more radiograph is always better regardless of clinical need
questions.explanation: Justification rests on the additional diagnostic and planning value of the 3-D dataset. The conversation should also transparently note CBCT’s imperfect sensitivity for the fracture line so the patient understands that definitive diagnosis may still require surgical inspection. ‘Always better’ or insurance-driven imaging violates ALARA and ethical imaging principles.

title: TMJ CBCT — Degenerative Joint Disease vs Normal Variation
short: 29F • Progressive anterior open bite • Bilateral TMJ crepitus

patient.medical_history: History of orthodontics as a teenager; no known systemic arthropathy.
patient.chief_complaint: My bite has been opening in the front over the last two years and I hear grinding in both joints.

clinical_findings.radiographs: CBCT shows bilateral flattened and irregular condylar contours, subchondral sclerosis, and osteophyte formation on the right. Joint spaces reduced. No evidence of acute fracture or ankylosis.

guidelines: Diagnostic criteria for degenerative joint disease

vignette.demographics: 29-year-old female with progressive anterior open bite.
vignette.chief: Worsening anterior open bite and bilateral crepitus.
vignette.clinical: Anterior open bite 3 mm. Maximum opening 42 mm with crepitus. No locking.
vignette.radio: CBCT: bilateral condylar flattening, sclerosis, right osteophyte; reduced joint space.

questions.q: According to DC/TMD and radiographic criteria, the CBCT findings are most consistent with which diagnosis?
options: Normal anatomic variation of the condyles
Degenerative joint disease (osteoarthrosis/osteoarthritis) of the TMJs
Acute condylar fracture
Rheumatoid arthritis until proven otherwise
